articles.title: Miss Bumbum Brasil: Gaúcha Cris Baldissera conquista o vice-campeonato | G1
articles.standfirst: Aplaudida de pé pelos jurados, empresária Cris Baldissera, 39 anos, de Butiá, desfilou ao som do clássico gaúcho durante concurso realizado em São Paulo em 15 de outubro.
articles.summary: A empresária Cris Baldissera, de Butiá, foi aplaudida de pé no Miss Bumbum Brasil ao desfilar com a bandeira do Rio Grande do Sul ao som de um clássico regional.
articles.body:
Desfilar com duas bandeiras do Rio Grande do Sul junto ao corpo foi a forma que a empreendedora Cris Baldissera, 39 anos, encontrou para valorizar a cultura gaúcha durante a 15ª edição do Miss Bumbum Brasil 2026, realizado em São Paulo, em 15 de outubro, na qual conquistou o título de vice-campeã .

Para esse momento, a gaúcha de Butiá escolheu como trilha musical a versão de Céu, Sol, Sul, Terra e Cor , interpretada pela conterrânea Luísa Sonza durante o programa Viver Sertanejo, apresentado pelo cantor Daniel, em 20 de setembro, na TV Globo. Acabou sendo aplaudida de pé pelos jurados.

"Meu maior orgulho foi poder representar meu estado e ter a consciência que cheguei nessa colocação com apresentações transparentes sem precisar pisar ou passar por cima de alguém", disse a empresária, que também atua como modelo para uma fábrica de lingerie de Minas Gerais.

Gaúcha vice-campeã do Miss Bumbum Brasil desfilou com bandeira do Rio Grande do Sul — Foto: Jamal Janry/Divulgação

Dona de uma loja de vestuário fitness e eleita Garota Verão por Butiá e São Jerônimo aos 15 e 16 anos, diz que a cultura regional está em suas origens.

"Grande parte da minha vida foi dentro de um CTG, cultuando as tradições, não perdia uma domingueira em Butiá. Então, carrego isso comigo e não importa onde eu esteja ou qual seja a situação, carregarei o Rio Grande do Sul sempre comigo", garante Cris, que é casada e não tem filhos.

articles.title: Como vivem indígenas da aldeia alvo de ameaças de envenenamento em MS | G1
articles.standfirst: Com quase 40% da população formada por indígenas, município do sul de MS tem duas importantes áreas Guarani-Kaiowá. Ameaça contra água consumida por moradores é investigada pelo MPF.
articles.summary: Com quase 40% da população formada por indígenas, município do sul de MS tem duas importantes áreas Guarani-Kaiowá. Ameaça contra água consumida por moradores é investigada.
articles.body:
A ameaça de envenenar a água consumida por indígenas em Tacuru , no sul de Mato Grosso do Sul, colocou em evidência a realidade das comunidades Guarani-Kaiowá que vivem no município, onde quase quatro em cada dez moradores são indígenas. O caso levou ao afastamento de servidores municipais e está sob investigação do Ministério Público Federal (MPF).

Até o momento, não foram encontrados indícios de que a água tenha sido envenenada. Em outra apuração, relacionada a denúncias de mortes na região, o MPF não encontrou elementos que confirmassem que as vítimas eram indígenas.

Mas a presença indígena em Tacuru e os conflitos enfrentados pelas comunidades são muito anteriores à repercussão do áudio. A história passa pela ocupação tradicional do território, pela criação de reservas, por reivindicações territoriais e, mais recentemente, por desafios relacionados ao acesso à água e à segurança.

Tacuru tem 10.808 habitantes, segundo o Censo de 2022. Desse total, 4.256 se declararam indígenas, o equivalente a aproximadamente 39,4% da população.

Duas áreas indígenas ficam no município: Sassoró e Jaguapiré , habitadas pelo povo Guarani-Kaiowá . Há ainda indígenas vivendo na área urbana. O coordenador regional da Fundação Nacional dos Povos Indígenas (Funai) em Ponta Porã, Tonico Benites, estima que entre 30 e 40 famílias indígenas morem na cidade.

Após ameaça de veneno na água, Força Nacional patrulha aldeias de MS — Foto: Ministério dos Povos Indígenas

Duas comunidades e uma história de ocupação

A Reserva Indígena Sassoró foi demarcada em 1928 pelo Serviço de Proteção aos Índios (SPI) e tem aproximadamente 1,9 mil hectares dentro do município. Dados do Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), com base em informações da Secretaria Especial de Saúde Indígena (Sesai), registraram 2.422 moradores na área em 2014.

Já a Terra Indígena Jaguapiré foi homologada em 1992 e tem cerca de 2,3 mil hectares. Segundo dados do Censo de 2022 reunidos pelo ISA, a área tinha 1.842 moradores indígenas.

A história dessas comunidades está ligada a um processo de mudanças na ocupação dos territórios indígenas em Mato Grosso do Sul. Entre 1915 e 1940, quando o estado ainda fazia parte de Mato Grosso, foram criadas reservas para concentrar grupos Guarani-Kaiowá em áreas delimitadas.

Sassoró está entre as áreas demarcadas nesse período. Com o passar dos anos, grupos indígenas passaram a reivindicar o retorno a territórios tradicionais, em um processo marcado por conflitos fundiários em diferentes regiões de Mato Grosso do Sul.

Entrada da cidade de Tacuru. — Foto: Reprodução/Facebook.

Para Matias Benno, coordenador do Conselho Indigenista Missionário (Cimi), os conflitos territoriais são uma das dimensões da violência enfrentada pelos Guarani-Kaiowá. Segundo ele, as comunidades também convivem com racismo, discriminação, assassinatos, atropelamentos e outras formas de violência.

O representante alerta que a violência contra os indígenas não começou após as eleições. Na avaliação dele, as manifestações de ódio no contexto político pós-eleitoral representam mais uma camada de um problema que já existia há décadas. A ameaça envolvendo a água em Tacuru, segundo Matias, é um exemplo de intimidação nesse cenário.

Ele também relata que o preconceito aparece no cotidiano, inclusive quando indígenas circulam pela cidade.

➡️A presença indígena também faz parte da identidade oficial do município. Desde 2010, o guarani é língua cooficial em Tacuru, ao lado do português. A Lei Municipal nº 848, de 18 de maio daquele ano, reconheceu o idioma e prevê o respeito às variedades guarani-kaiowá, mbya e ñandeva.

➡️➡️A legislação também estabelece medidas para ampliar o uso da língua indígena em serviços e ações públicas, como atendimentos básicos de saúde e campanhas de prevenção.

Ameaça contra a água muda rotina em Sassoró

O episódio que levou o município ao centro das atenções começou com a divulgação de um áudio com ameaças contra indígenas, incluindo a intenção de envenenar a água consumida pela comunidade.

Na Aldeia Sassoró, aproximadamente 98% das casas têm água encanada, segundo o cacique Ivan Montiel, que também é vereador em Tacuru. A comunidade é abastecida por poços artesianos e, normalmente, não depende de caminhões-pipa.

Quando há problemas, como a quebra de uma bomba, a prefeitura é acionada para garantir o fornecimento de água até que o abastecimento seja restabelecido.

Apesar de a maior parte das residências ter acesso à água encanada, a ameaça provocou medo entre os moradores. Segundo Montiel, a preocupação ultrapassa a possibilidade de contaminação e atinge a rotina das famílias.

“Estamos vivendo um clima de medo e insegurança. Como liderança, temos lutado para que a comunidade possa recuperar a tranquilidade e voltar à sua rotina normal”, afirmou.

O cacique relata que moradores estão receosos de deixar a aldeia para ir à cidade e realizar atividades cotidianas. “O medo não está relacionado apenas à questão da água, mas também à segurança das famílias e à liberdade de ir e vir”, disse.

Para ele, a comunidade quer retomar a rotina sem ameaças.

“O nosso povo quer viver em paz, com segurança e dignidade, sem precisar ter medo de sair de suas casas ou de circular pelo município.”

O Ministério Público Federal acompanha o caso. O procurador da República Marco Antônio Delfino de Almeida informou ao g1 que a investigação continua em andamento no gabinete do 6º Ofício da Procuradoria da República em Dourados. Até o momento, não foram encontrados indícios de que a água tenha sido envenenada.

O procurador explicou que o MPF também acompanha denúncias de ameaças contra comunidades indígenas e quilombolas em Mato Grosso do Sul. Segundo ele, situações desse tipo podem ser apuradas nas esferas criminal e cível quando há indícios de crimes de ódio e racismo.

Dois servidores municipais foram afastados após a repercussão do caso. Segundo o procurador do município, a prefeitura instaurou um Processo Administrativo Disciplinar (PAD) e informou ao MPF que está tomando as providências cabíveis.

Segundo a prefeitura, os dois afastados são motoristas: um trabalha com caminhão-caçamba, na área de infraestrutura, e o outro atua na coleta de resíduos, ligada ao setor de meio ambiente. A administração municipal afirma que nenhum deles tem relação com o abastecimento de água.

🔎Mato Grosso do Sul tem conselhos comunitários de segurança implantados em 17 comunidades indígenas, sendo dois em Campo Grande e 15 no interior, segundo a Secretaria de Estado de Justiça e Segurança Pública (Sejusp). Os representantes são escolhidos pelas próprias comunidades e atuam no diálogo e na busca por soluções para problemas locais, respeitando a organização e a cultura de cada povo.

Ministros Eloy Terena, Janine Mello e Wellington César Lima e Silva seguem para MS após ameaças a indígenas — Foto: Reprodução

Força Nacional patrulha aldeias e ministros vão a MS

Após as denúncias, a Força Nacional de Segurança Pública começou a patrulhar comunidades indígenas de Mato Grosso do Sul, entre elas Sassoró, em Tacuru.

O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) determinou o envio de uma comitiva com três ministros a Mato Grosso do Sul para acompanhar de perto as denúncias de ameaças contra comunidades indígenas. A decisão foi anunciada pelo ministro dos Povos Indígenas, Eloy Terena, em entrevista ao g1 .

Além de Eloy Terena, a comitiva é formada pela ministra dos Direitos Humanos e da Cidadania, Janine Mello, e pelo ministro da Justiça e Segurança Pública, Wellington César Lima e Silva.

Neste sábado (31), a previsão é que visitem duas comunidades indígenas: a aldeia Taquapiri, em Coronel Sapucaia, e a aldeia Sassoró, em Tacuru.

Casa de Reza na Aldeia Sassoró, em Tacuru (MS). — Foto: Reprodução/Edson Lopes

Outros casos de violência registrados em aldeias de MS

Além da investigação em Tacuru, a Polícia Civil registrou recentemente outras ocorrências envolvendo indígenas em Mato Grosso do Sul.

Os casos aconteceram em municípios diferentes e têm investigações próprias. Até o momento, não há informação de ligação entre essas ocorrências e a ameaça investigada em Tacuru.

Morte na Aldeia Porto Lindo, em Japorã: na madrugada de sexta-feira (30), a Polícia Civil foi comunicada, às 2h53, sobre a localização do corpo de Damácio Moraes, de 40 anos, sob as arquibancadas do estádio de futebol da comunidade. A vítima apresentava lesões aparentes na cabeça e no pescoço. A polícia e a perícia foram ao local, e o corpo foi encaminhado ao Instituto de Medicina e Odontologia Legal (IMOL) de Naviraí para exame necroscópico. Até o registro da ocorrência, não haviam sido identificadas testemunhas presenciais nem câmeras nas proximidades. As circunstâncias da morte seguem sob investigação.

Lesão corporal na Aldeia Te’yikue, em Caarapó: na noite de quarta-feira (28), por volta das 20h50, um indígena de 36 anos foi ferido durante uma agressão. Segundo as informações da ocorrência, duas mulheres indígenas, ainda não identificadas, são apontadas como autoras. O homem teria sido atingido com um objeto e precisou ser levado ao hospital.

articles.title: Chapa eleita no AC abre discussão para mais mulheres na política | G1
articles.standfirst: Em contraponto às eleições para governo do Acre, Assembleia Legislativa não terá mulheres entre as 24 cadeiras a serem ocupadas a partir do próximo ano. Cientista político diz que chegada ao Executivo pode seguir caminhos diferentes e que Legislativo ainda é espaço menos acessível.
articles.summary: No estado, duas mulheres foram eleitas para o governo, mas em contrapartida, Aleac terá apenas homens a partir de 2017. Cientista político analisa próximo cenário.
articles.body:
Chapa formada por Mailza Assis (PP) e Jéssica Sales (MDB) foi eleita nas Eleições 2026 — Foto: Arquivo/Asscom

A chapa formada por Mailza Assis ( PP ) e Jéssica Sales ( MDB ), que venceu o segundo turno das Eleições 2026, assume o comando do estado a partir do próximo ano. Embora seja uma composição inédita para o Palácio Rio Branco , ambas devem lidar, durante quatro anos, com uma assembleia legislativa composta 100% por homens.

👉 Contexto: Mailza será a primeira mulher a governar o Acre pelo voto direto e, junto a Jéssica, formaram a primeira chapa 100% feminina a vencer o pleito que ocorreu no último dia 25 de outubro. A governabilidade delas terá como um dos pontos centrais a relação com a Assembleia Legislativa do Acre (Aleac) onde das 24 cadeiras disputadas, nenhuma será ocupada por mulheres .

Ao g1 , o professor e cientista político Nilson Euclides detalhou que a eleição inédita de uma chapa inteiramente feminina para comandar o Executivo do estado abre espaço para discutir a participação e inclusão das mulheres na política acreana.

“Por um lado, você teve a eleição de uma governadora com a sua vice, ou seja, uma chapa feminina, que saiu vencedora nas eleições para governo do Estado em 2026. Por outro lado, você tem uma eleição para o poder legislativo esvaziada da figura feminina. São 24 deputados e não há nenhuma mulher, nenhuma representante feminina”, frisou.

Para o cientista, essa diferença revela que o acesso das mulheres a esses cargos , no caso do Executivo e do Legislativo, pode ocorrer por caminhos distintos .

“Nessa questão, temos mulheres que são alçadas para dentro do mundo da política, mas que tem essa entrada não por uma militância, por estar envolvida em movimentos populares por serem lideranças populares ou serem lideranças políticas construídas dentro desse embate político-partidário ou do movimento social”, detalhou.

Por outro lado, segundo ele, a conquista de uma cadeira no Parlamento exige a construção de uma trajetória eleitoral e partidária.

“A gente consegue entender a dificuldade que se tem na Assembleia Legislativa de ter figuras femininas justamente porque, na Aleac, o caminho para se chegar a uma cadeira ou é via partido ou por ser membro de uma família tradicional da política ou ser militante de um movimento, estar envolvida em algum tipo de luta política, seja ela popular ou mais partidária e orgânica”, acrescentou.

Mailza Assis, 1ª governadora do Acre eleita por voto direto da história do estado — Foto: Jhenyfer de Souza/g1

Conforme o cientista político, a eleição de uma chapa formada por mulheres para comandar o Acre precisa ser observada também a partir das trajetórias políticas de Mailza e Jéssica . Nilson cita ainda os vínculos familiares e as alianças tradicionais como fatores que podem facilitar a entrada de mulheres na política institucional.

A primeira governadora do estado, Iolanda Fleming, que chefiou o estado entre 1986 e 1987, também se enquadraria neste contexto, visto que ela era esposa de Geraldo Fleming, ex-deputado federal. Iolanda foi vereadora de Rio Branco, vice-prefeita da Capital e deputada estadual antes de comandar o Acre.

Para o professor, a presença de conexões com grupos políticos já estabelecidos é uma característica que ajuda a compreender o porquê a conquista do Executivo pode ocorrer sem que haja uma ampliação equivalente da representação feminina no Legislativo.

“Então, nessa questão, ou seja, para você entrar nesse espaço legislativo, o caminho me parece um pouco mais difícil para as mulheres não só no Acre, como no Brasil, porque é um caminho que, antes de chegar na Assembleia Legislativa, é preciso entrar em outros espaços que são muito masculinizados ”, disse.

Segundo Nilson, partidos políticos e movimentos sociais precisam criar condições para que lideranças femininas construídas em espaços comunitários, periferias, conselhos e outras instituições também conquistem visibilidade e oportunidades de disputar eleições .

O cientista pontua, todavia, que a participação nas estruturas partidárias e nos espaços de decisão ainda representa um desafio para as mulheres que buscam transformar sua atuação social em candidaturas competitivas.

““As mulheres lideram alguns processos, mas dificilmente essa liderança chega a ser algo que se constitua como uma liderança política ou partidária [...] Essa é uma questão que precisa ser bem estudada e analisada para que as mulheres possam, por meio das lutas coletivas que elas imprimem na sociedade, se constituírem como lideranças, mas não apenas lideranças oriundas de famílias tradicionais ou de indicações”, disse.

A proposta, de acordo com o cientista político, é ampliar as possibilidades de participação e fortalecer trajetórias próprias dentro das organizações políticas “para que essa representação seja genuinamente construída no seio dessa luta popular, democrática, dentro dos partidos, dos movimentos sociais e, claramente, das outras instituições representativas”, finalizou.

Veja a composição da Assembleia Legislativa do Acre a partir de 2027 — Foto: Reprodução

Com a análise, o cientista pontua que a gestão de Mailza tem dois aspectos relevantes a partir de 2027: a capacidade de construir apoio na Assembleia Legislativa e o significado político de uma chapa feminina no comando do governo do estado , onde a nova composição legislativa não terá mulheres eleitas.

No cenário do próximo ano, com base nas projeções de alianças e declarações de apoio, a maioria dos parlamentares estarão alinhados, ou seja, vão compor a base do governo, uma condição inicial favorável para a articulação política.

Já na oposição, com menor número de representantes, estão: Eduardo Ribeiro (Republicanos), Gene Diniz (Republicanos), Emerson Jarude (Novo), Edvaldo Magalhães (PCdoB), Tadeu Hassem (Republicanos), Jailson Amorim (PSD) e Antônio Pedro (PSD).

Todos estes partidos, em algum momento da disputa eleitoral deste ano, apoiaram candidatos de oposição à gestão eleita.

articles.title: Primeiro-ministro britânico admite pedido de desculpas pela escravidão | G1
articles.standfirst: Declaração ocorre às vésperas de cúpula da Commonwealth, na qual líderes caribenhos devem pressionar o Reino Unido por compensações financeiras pelo comércio de escravos.
articles.summary: Declaração ocorre às vésperas de cúpula da Commonwealth, na qual líderes caribenhos devem pressionar o Reino Unido por compensações financeiras pelo comércio de escravos.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham — Foto: AP Photo/Kin Cheung, Pool

O primeiro-ministro britânico, Andy Burnham, afirmou estar aberto à possibilidade de apresentar um pedido formal de desculpas pelo papel histórico do Reino Unido na escravidão.

A declaração ocorre antes da cúpula da Commonwealth, prevista para a próxima semana, na qual ele deve enfrentar pressões por reparações financeiras.

Em artigo publicado no jornal The Guardian, Burnham afirmou que a Grã-Bretanha estava "oferecendo um diálogo estruturado com aqueles afetados pelo comércio transatlântico de escravos".

Nesse período, pelo menos 12,5 milhões de africanos foram sequestrados e vendidos como escravos.

"Ouvir os apelos por um pedido formal de desculpas em nome do Estado britânico será uma parte importante deste processo, e estou aberto a eles", acrescentou.

Burnham, porém, rejeitou os pedidos de reparação financeira. "Não creio que o povo britânico de hoje possa ser responsabilizado por erros históricos, por mais hediondos que sejam, que ocorreram numa época diferente, sob leis diferentes e nos quais não tiveram qualquer participação pessoal", escreveu.

Entre os séculos XV e XIX, milhões de africanos foram vendidos como escravos por comerciantes europeus.

Desse total, cerca de 3,2 milhões foram transportados pela Grã-Bretanha através do Oceano Atlântico, segundo o Banco de Dados do Comércio Transatlântico de Escravos.

Antes da reunião de chefes de governo da Commonwealth, prevista para a próxima semana em Antígua e Barbuda, o rei Charles, que está em visita ao Caribe, afirmou que "é justo reconhecermos o grande sofrimento e as injustiças do passado".

A expectativa é que os líderes caribenhos pressionem por reparações, que podem incluir redução de dívidas, recursos para o desenvolvimento, educação, saúde e medidas para enfrentar os efeitos das mudanças climáticas.

Burnham também escreveu no Guardian que pretendia "lançar uma nova campanha em relação à dívida", com medidas para ajudar os países mais vulneráveis a "pagarem suas dívidas ao longo de um período mais longo e com taxas melhores".

O primeiro-ministro de Antígua e Barbuda, Gaston Browne, recebeu positivamente as declarações de Burnham e suas propostas de ajuda aos países afetados.

No entanto, ressaltou, em uma publicação no Facebook, que a posição histórica dos países caribenhos sobre as reparações permanece inalterada.

articles.title: Halloween nas escolas de Tatuí: lei proíbe festas e atividades | G1
articles.standfirst: Lei que proíbe atividades de Halloween nas escolas foi promulgada pela Câmara em março deste ano. Pesquisador afirma que a proibição pode limitar o trabalho dos professores e o processo de aprendizagem.
articles.summary: Halloween nas escolas de Tatuí é proibido por lei municipal que visa proteger tradições, mas especialistas alertam para prejuízos no aprendizado dos alunos.
articles.body:
O Dia das Bruxas - ou Halloween - é celebrado neste sábado (31) e, neste ano, as escolas municipais de Tatuí (SP) não terão atividades ou festas relacionadas ao tema devido a uma proibição prevista em lei.

O projeto de lei foi aprovado pela Câmara Municipal em fevereiro deste ano e promulgado em março , após o prefeito da cidade, Professor Miguel ( PSD ), não se manifestar dentro do prazo legal.

Segundo a lei, fica proibido toda e qualquer atividade relacionada à cultura do Dia das Bruxas, como festas, decorações ou comemorações dentro das escolas . A iniciativa, proposta pelo vereador Renan Cortez ( MDB ), diz proteger os valores éticos e familiares dos estudantes, além de valorizar o folclore brasileiro.

Escolas municipais de Tatuí não terão atividades de Halloween por proibição legislativa — Foto: Prefeitura de Tatuí/Divulgação

Andriolli Costa, jornalista e pesquisador especializado em folclore e cultura popular brasileira, avalia a medida como uma "posição curiosa". Segundo ele, existe uma desigualdade de espaço entre o Halloween e as figuras nacionais, mas, a proibição não faria, necessariamente, alguém gostar do folclore local de imediato.

"Como pesquisador, argumento sempre a favor do Dia do Saci ou de uma convivência com o Dia das Bruxas, ainda que tensionadora. A indústria cultural norte-americana tem uma força que nossos contadores de histórias e artistas não conseguem acompanhar, mas, proibir o Halloween não resolve isso. Tirar a abóbora da escola não faz com que alguém passe a gostar do saci", opina.

O profissional prossegue, dizendo que, para entender o ocorrido na cidade, é necessário refletir de forma diferente. Ao contrário do Halloween, ele diz que as figuras folclóricas, como o saci-pererê, são uma oportunidade de conhecimento cultural nacional.

"Diante do ocorrido em Tatuí, é preciso um outro exercício de reflexão. Defendo o Dia do Saci porque quero que as crianças tenham mais opirtunidades de conhecer e se encantar com a cultura popular brasileira. Existe uma desigualdade de espaço entre as duas datas", pontua.

Montagem com Saci e elementos do Halloween. — Foto: reprodução

Na visão de Andriolli, a proposta não garante que a proibição do Dia das Bruxas tenha acontecido com o intuito de valorizar o folclore brasileiro - apesar disso ser dito pelo autor do projeto de lei. Segundo ele, o argumento do documento é apenas "evitar temas sombrios para não assustar crianças".

Ele aponta que o medo é um sentimento como qualquer outros e que a criança simboliza a partir do imaginário.

"Somos apresentados aos 'monstros invisíveis' do ciclo do medo infantil, como cucas, papões e outros que habitam tanto as cantigas de ninar quanto as sombras do quarto. Quando crescemos, deixam de ser apenas criaturas que comem e descomem, mas sim sobre formas de experienciar outros sentimentos a partir da narrativa", diz.

Ao g1 , o pesquisador faz um contraponto em comparação às figuras nacionais: o Dia das Bruxas pode, também, render atividades pedagógicas e aprendizados. Ele sugere que o tema pode ser aproveitado para revisitar lendas urbanas da comunidade.

"O Halloween pode ser muitas coisas, como entretenimento, indústria cultural ou até prática esvaziada, mas pode render boas atividades, dependendo da forma como os professores trabalham o tema. Por que não aproveitar o momento para revisitar lendas urbanas da comunidade, que revelam muito da formação histórica e social do nosso território?", questiona.

Raimundão, Dama de Branco e Cobra Grande: lendas atravessam gerações em Itapetininga (SP) — Foto: Jaime Rafael/TV TEM

Andriolli diz que a conversa com familiares pode ser uma forma de partir de um interesse que já existe e ampliar o repertório sobre o assunto. Já uma festa realizada pode ser a etapa final de uma atividade de pesquisa.

"Fazer a festa pode ser uma etapa final de uma pesquisa. Como são as bruxas brasileiras? o que Matinta Pereira, do norte, tem de diferente da Pisadeira, que 'perturba o sono' no sudeste? e no caso do Dia do Saci, seria possível pensar em uma atividade que mistura o Halloween com a data brasileira?", aponta.

Para o pesquisador, a proibição pode limitar a atuação dos professores e reduzir as oportunidades de aprendizagem dos alunos.

"Uma proibição tão ampla pode limitar o trabalho dos professores e fechar possibilidades de aprendizagem. Se queremos fortalecer a cultura brasileira, precisamos oferecer bons materiais, apoiar educadores e aproximar as escolas das pessoas que mantêm esses saberes vivos. São oportunidades de despertar essa curiosidade", conclui Andriolli.

Em nota enviada ao g1 nesta sexta-feira (30), a Prefeitura de Tatuí afirmou que valoriza os aspectos da cultura nacional e geral, com os índices educacionais da cidade mostrando um desempenho sólido no ensino básico.

A administração municipal não informou se pretende incluir no calendário letivo outras atividades para substituir as relacionadas ao Halloween.

Renan Cortez afirma, como justificativa, que o Halloween não tem relação com a cultura brasileira e argumenta que a celebração pode interferir negativamente no ambiente escolar, ao "promover valores e práticas que não são alinhados com a nossa identidade cultural".

O parlamentar também justifica que a proposta busca incentivar a cultura de paz nas escolas. Segundo ele, a festividade envolve elementos ligados ao medo e a temas sombrios, que podem causar desconforto e até assustar crianças, especialmente as mais sensíveis a esse tipo de estímulo.

Câmara Municipal de Tatuí — Foto: Reprodução/TV TEM

Durante a apresentação do projeto no plenário da Câmara, Renan Cortez pediu o apoio dos demais vereadores para a aprovação da proposta, afirmando ser cristão, pai de família e educador.

Segundo ele, a iniciativa também representa um posicionamento dos parlamentares sobre o que consideram “efetivo, benéfico e correto” para ser aplicado na rede municipal de ensino. Assista ao vídeo no início da reportagem.

"Se nós temos que começar a comemorar um dia na rede municipal de ensino, seria o dia do Senhor Jesus, do todo poderoso, do senhor nosso Deus. Esse é o meu posicionamento e a minha opinião", destacou o parlamentar no plenário.

Com a oficialização da lei, a prefeitura deveria promover, por meio da Secretaria de Educação, ações para conscientizar os alunos sobre a importância de valorizar e respeitar as tradições brasileiras, destacando a diversidade e a riqueza das festas culturais do país.

À época, o g1 procurou a Prefeitura de Tatuí para obter esclarecimentos sobre o tema, mas não teve retorno.

articles.title: After the ‘martyr’s’ funeral: The families left behind by Yemen’s war
articles.summary: Rising fatalities in Yemen’s conflict deepen the burden on families of fighters, both emotionally and financially.
articles.body:
Sanaa, Yemen – Pickups carrying the bodies of Houthi fighters occasionally travel through the streets of Sanaa. Alongside them in the back, gunmen accompany the fallen fighters on their final journey to the cemetery.

A song known as “Our martyrs are our greats” echoes loudly from the moving vehicles, drawing the attention of passersby. At the cemetery, mourners solemnly pay their respects to the fallen fighters and show solidarity with their families.

Funerals of fighters have been a recurring sight in Yemen over the past few weeks.

Earlier this month, the Yemeni government said its forces killed or wounded 1,540 Houthis in 24 hours. Last week, the government said 16,100 Houthi operatives and commanders had been killed or wounded since October 5.

Houthis have also killed hundreds of pro-government troops over the past few weeks, with an October 19 missile attack on a security camp in Shabwa killing more than 70 government soldiers.

While the families of the deceased fighters receive fleeting public tributes at cemeteries, their grief and loss endure long after the funerals. For them, life has become more difficult, economic hardships have deepened and sorrow is a constant companion.

“The martyrdom of my brother, Abdulaziz, on October 10 broke us and robbed us of peace of mind. We could smile to hide our pain, but our hearts are filled with bottomless grief,” Akram, a 23-year-old resident of Sanaa, told Al Jazeera.

Abdulaziz, 21, was killed in Dhubab, in southwestern Yemen, while fighting alongside the Houthi group, two months after being recruited, Akram said.

Before Abdulaziz went to the front line, the two brothers worked in Sanaa as daily-wage workers in construction or agriculture. When they managed to get work, they pooled their earnings to cover the living expenses of their six-member family. That made the family’s financial difficulties “manageable”, said Akram.

Today, he struggles without his brother and covering the family’s basic needs has become a harder task.

“I lost my pillar of strength, Abdulaziz. His income, along with mine, used to cover water, electricity and food expenses. Without him, I am like a bird with one wing, burdened by so many responsibilities,” said Akram.

Over the past few days, petrol and diesel prices have risen by 10 percent in Houthi-controlled northwestern Yemen, adding to the cost of basic goods and increasing pressure on struggling families, such as Akram’s.

“When it comes to paying the fees for water, electricity, or buying groceries, it does not matter if your relative is a martyr or not. You have to pay or starve to death,” said Akram.

In recent months, Yemen has faced a major escalation in fighting between Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-aligned Houthi group that controls parts of the country.

The latest escalation “threatens to be absolutely devastating” for food security , said the World Food Programme’s Assistant Executive Director for Programme Operations, Matthew Hollingworth, earlier this month.

“We are looking at a hunger crisis that is going to grow as it persists,” Hollingworth added.

The Houthis seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in September 2014 and subsequently took control of much of northern and western Yemen. Since then, the conflict has remained unresolved.

Like many other deceased fighters’ families in Houthi-controlled areas, Houthi authorities gave Akram’s family a food basket, which included flour, cooking oil, rice and sugar.

However, the supply of food or financial assistance is irregular, Sanaa-based Ali Yahia, a 55-year-old father of a deceased fighter, told Al Jazeera.

“My son was killed four years ago on the Saudi-Yemen border when he was fighting for the Sanaa-based government. Since then, I have received food baskets at different times. Sometimes, I receive them twice a year or thrice a year, or four times a year,” he said.

For Yahia, this support is insufficient, and he argues that “fair compensation” would be a monthly salary of $200 at least. “This amount of money would help a family cover the basics each month,” he said.

Yahia has two other sons who support him. One is a delivery rider in Sanaa and the other works at a restaurant.

“With their support, my living conditions have improved. But if a family depends on a fighter’s income, the death of the fighter sparks a living and psychological ordeal for the whole family,” he said.

According to the World Food Programme, 18.3 million people across Yemen face severe food insecurity, while 2.2 million children under five suffer from acute malnutrition.

As the number of fighters killed on the front lines rises, the authorities’ ability to support bereaved families is increasingly stretched, Ali Mohammed, a Houthi representative in Sanaa, told Al Jazeera.

“Martyrs today are too many and their families deserve due support. However, the rising number of martyrs affects the level of support they receive. Assistance is distributed so that every family gets some,” said Mohammed.

He argued that the “complete Houthi victory will lead to stability in the country and this will give authorities a better opportunity to look after the families of the martyrs.” He added: “This will take time”.

On October 25, the Sanaa-based Houthi Ministry of Youth and Sports commemorated Martyrs’ Day in the presence of many Houthi officials.

During the event, the group’s Undersecretary for the Sports Sector, Ali Hadban, emphasised the importance of observing the occasion to “draw inspiration from the lessons of sacrifice and selflessness, and to reflect on the enduring legacies of the martyrs who defended the nation”.

He noted that the victories achieved across various fronts are the direct result of the sacrifices made by “these noble martyrs”, emphasising the need to provide support and care for their families.

At the end of 2021, the UN estimated that 377,000 people had been killed directly or indirectly by the war in Yemen. The recent return of fighting has claimed more lives.

Adel Dashela, researcher at the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies, described the public celebration of fallen fighters as “an alien practice” that emerged during the war.

“This practice reflects the normalisation of violence and encourages children to risk their lives and die under various sectarian and political slogans. Yemenis did not witness this phenomenon until the Houthi group took control of the capital, Sanaa,” Dashela told Al Jazeera.

Families may be encouraged to participate in these rituals and may find themselves compelled to do so under social and political pressure, he said. “The reality, however, is that public displays of honour do not alleviate families’ suffering. Instead, the social, psychological and financial consequences of their loss remain their burden to bear.”

In many cases, women and children assume responsibility for supporting their families after the death of the breadwinner.

“Thus, women and children bear the real cost of these losses, while public celebrations remain detached from their everyday realities and the ongoing suffering of bereaved families,” Dashela added.

articles.title: Call for National Lottery to join GAMSTOP after Bedfordshire death
articles.summary: A coroner says there is a risk of further deaths unless the National Lottery is included in the scheme.
articles.body:
A coroner has called for the National Lottery to be included in a self-exclusion gambling scheme after a man with a gambling addiction took his own life.

Stephen Goff, 54, died from asphyxiation at his flat in Leighton Buzzard, Bedfordshire, on 18 August 2025, an inquest heard.

Emma Whitting, senior coroner for Bedfordshire and Luton, said there was a risk of further deaths unless the National Lottery draw was covered by GAMSTOP.

The system prevents people who register with it from accessing gambling websites and apps licensed in Great Britain.

The coroner has sent the Prevention of Future Deaths (PFD) report to the Gambling Commission and GAMSTOP.

A spokesperson for the commission said that following the inquest, they had "been working with Gamstop and Allwyn, the National Lottery operator, to consider whether further protections are needed in this area".

The inquest heard that since 2006, Goff had struggled with gambling addiction, which led to the breakdown of his marriage the following year.

Despite self-excluding from all online licensed gambling operators in 2018 and again in 2024 via GAMSTOP, he continued to gamble online with the National Lottery Draw.

His last bank payment from his almost depleted account was to the National Lottery Draw.

His body was found on his sofa on 18 August 2025, and a post-mortem examination concluded that he had died from asphyxiation.

The coroner concluded he died as a result of suicide.

In her PFD report, she raised concerns that by "not including online gambling with the National Lottery Draw in the GAMSTOP scheme, there was a risk that consumers having self-excluded via GAMSTOP will still gamble online with the National Lottery Draw".

Goff's daughter, Freya, said they welcomed the coroner's PFD report, "which highlights the glaring omission that National Lottery gaming products are not covered by the GAMSTOP self-exclusion scheme".

A Gambling Commission spokesperson said that "although National Lottery draw-based games are generally lower risk when compared against other gambling products, we will consider the potential for further changes, including the possibility of extending the scope of Gamstop in some form".

articles.title: Skiddaw Forest peatland being restored in £500,000 project
articles.summary: Cumbria Wildlife Trust starts work repairing damage to Skiddaw Forest's peatland.
articles.body:
Work has started on a project to restore 435 hectares (1,077 acres) of damaged peatland.

Cumbria Wildlife Trust will carry out the work in Skiddaw Forest where it will also repair a 6km (3.7-mile) boundary fence.

The forest is home to one of the largest continuous areas of blanket bog in the Lake District and acts as a huge carbon store.

Peatland team manager for the trust Susie Webb said: "Once improved, the peatlands will also slow the flow of water off the fells, which will help protect local communities downstream from flooding and will benefit a huge variety of wildlife."

The project is expected to take between three and four months but public access to Skiddaw Forest won't be affected.

Webb said: "We expect to see an increase in specialist plants such as sundews and sphagnum mosses and greater numbers of dragonflies.

"Birds such as snipe, which live on wet grassland, marshes and moorlands, will benefit from the rewetted ground."

articles.title: How do you navigate Halloween with food allergies?
articles.summary: BBC News NI speaks to people about how they navigate their allergies at Halloween.
articles.body:
Like a lot of other holidays, food often plays a big part in how people celebrate Halloween, but it can be a more complex to navigate if you have a food allergy - especially if you want to go to parties or take children trick or treating.

How do people with allergies ensure they can take part in the fun and stay safe? And how can you help make sure that everyone is included in the celebrations?

Ciara, 15, is allergic to milk and eggs.

"You have to make sure you read every packet of everything, and you couldn't eat anything until you got home so that you were safe and you were sure of what was happening," she said.

When it comes to Halloween, she said people having more awareness would mean that everyone could be included in the fun.

She says that her friend group really help her by knowing about her allergies and what to do if she was to have a reaction.

Whilst she said it "wasn't easy" or a "particularly enjoyable" thing to do, she taught her group what to do in an emergency situation.

Ciara carries EpiPens. These are adrenaline injections that can help to save people's lives in a serious allergic reaction.

The 15-year-old explained that Halloween can be a bit more difficult to navigate.

She described how a lot of people are helpful and understanding about allergies but sometimes, "there are other people that just don't seem to fully understand the consequences" of what would happen if she was exposed to what she's allergic to.

Her mum, Claire McGuigan, said she is proud of how well Ciara deals with her allergy.

She explained that parents of children with allergies have all the usual worries but "first and foremost is your allergy".

"As a parent, you carry all that worry and you just hope that they go out and they have a nice time and they come back safe, full of fun, and they can forget about their allergies as much as they can for that night".

"I think having a good circle of friends who understands the allergies is important.

"Trying to prevent the harm rather than relying on the rescue medication is really, really important," she continued.

Ciara's mum described the emotional burden on families and called for a national conversation about it.

She said people who have children with allergies or have allergies themselves have to do their "best to navigate a whole world that wasn't designed for you".

"I think take your wins everyday that you're safe and that you're happy and don't let it define you. You can be who you want to be," she continued.

She believes that with "a bit of careful planning" children with allergies can feel included.

'Understood but not made to feel different'

Caolán has just turned 11. His mum Colette Donaghy said he does all the "school activities that you could name" and he's "mad into scooting".

Caolán is allergic to nuts, dairy and eggs and has had, in the past, a very serious anaphylactic reaction that resulted in him being in an induced coma in intensive care.

"He has an awareness and a knowledge and probably a risk awareness that many other children of his age wouldn't have," his mum said.

She thinks it's important that children with allergies are "understood" but not made to feel "really different".

When it comes to Halloween, Donaghy explained that when Caolán trick or treats, he waits until the end when all the other children have been given their sweets.

"Then he will explain to the people at the door that he has allergies and there's only certain things he can have. And then, of course, before he would eat anything, we would have to check it," she said.

Donaghy advised giving out individually wrapped sweets to help avoid cross-contamination.

She also suggested looking at alternatives to sweets like fruit or little toys "that don't cost very much".

"There's loads of different options for people and that would take away another layer of anxiety for parents," she said.

Donaghy also explained how some people use teal pumpkins to indicate that a house will offer treats that are suitable for any trick-or-treaters who have any food allergies or intolerances.

Niamh Kennedy has three children who have food allergies and she is the chair of Food Allergy NI. It's a group aiming to build a safer and more inclusive society for everyone affected by food allergies.

She said special occasions are often centred around food.

"For families living with food allergies, these celebrations can bring an extra layer of planning and worry that many people never have to think about."

She explained that "every item may need to be checked and every situation assessed for risk".

How can you make sure everyone's included?

Kennedy suggests that everyone should "think ahead" to consider how they can make celebrations inclusive.

She said this may include "offering non-food alternatives, providing clear ingredient information, communicating with families in advance and being mindful of the risk of cross-contact".

"Being thoughtful and understanding can make a real difference to whether someone feels left out or included in these occasions."

articles.title: How books saved Birmingham author Kit de Waal from breakdown
articles.summary: Birmingham author Kit de Waal says a chance conversation changed her life after she left home at 16.
articles.body:
International bestselling author Kit de Waal has told the BBC how a chance conversation changed her life after she left home at 16, struggled with drugs and found herself on the brink of a serious mental breakdown.

The Birmingham-born writer said she was "a couple of months away from a very serious breakdown" before a solicitor's reading recommendation changed the course of her life.

Speaking to BBC Upload, she said: "I found the world of reading, the world of imagination.

Born in Birmingham to an Irish mother and a Caribbean father, de Waal grew up in Moseley at a time when mixed-race families were rare.

"My father came over from the Caribbean in 1956 and my mother is an Irish immigrant," she said.

The family lived on the edge of a predominantly middle-class area, but de Waal said her childhood was marked by poverty.

"We were very, very poor. I was brought up in poverty, there's no other way about it."

She said those experiences later became central to her writing.

"What I learnt from it was difference, what it's like to be an outsider, what it's like to be poor, hungry, lost, not fit in, the damage that poverty does, the damage that racism does to children."

Yet she also remembers acts of kindness.

After her family moved into a largely white neighbourhood, one neighbour invited the children into their home to see their pet tortoise.

"I learnt from that the power of kindness and the profound effect it has when other people aren't being kind."

When she was six, her mother became a Jehovah's Witness.

De Waal left home at 16 after deciding she no longer wanted to follow the faith.

"I was wild," she said. "I took a lot of drugs, drank a lot, did everything you can imagine."

The deaths of friends from heroin overdoses forced her to confront where her life was heading.

By the age of 21, she said her mental health had deteriorated badly.

"I would say a couple of months away from a very serious breakdown."

After returning home and finding work with the Crown Prosecution Service, an off-hand comment from a solicitor would prove life-changing.

Seeing her yawn during a meeting, he suggested reading to help with her insomnia.

At the time, de Waal said she disliked books and had never developed a reading habit.

The solicitor gave her a list of 10 novels, including War and Peace and Madame Bovary.

"I've never cured the insomnia," she said.

Reading became a lifelong passion and eventually inspired her to start writing herself.

Despite believing she could write a novel in a matter of months, de Waal said it took more than a decade of rejection and learning the craft before she was published.

Her breakthrough came with My Name Is Leon, the story of a young boy in the care system growing up in 1980s Birmingham.

The novel became an international bestseller and was later adapted by the BBC after Sir Lenny Henry, who narrated the audiobook, became determined to bring the story to the screen.

Yet de Waal said the most important lesson from her success was a simple one.

"If there's a lesson, it's write the thing you really care about."

Now one of Britain's best-known authors, she remains a passionate advocate for reading in all its forms, including audiobooks.

Despite an international career, she still credits reading with changing the direction of her life.

"I found the world of reading," she said.

articles.title: North East tourism tax backlash: 'Rothbury is not Edinburgh'
articles.summary: Businesses say the North East Mayor's tax plans are a bad idea, but she says they will create jobs.
articles.body:
Hotels and music venues have hit out a mayor's plans to introduce a tourism tax.

In September , the government confirmed plans to allow local leaders to introduce a levy targeted at tourists staying in hotels, bed and breakfasts and other types of accommodation in their regions.

North East Mayor Kim McGuinness has said she will bring in the fee and it would boost jobs, while Tees Valley Mayor Ben Houchen has said he will not. Local authorities within McGuinness's jurisdiction have also attacked plans for the levy.

Newcastle music venue owner Kate Hodgkinson said McGuinness's tax plans were ill-thought out, while Rothbury landlord Debbie Noble said they would put visitors off.

Variations of the tourism tax already exist in parts of the UK.

In Scotland local authorities can charge a visitor levy on overnight accommodation.

For example, in Edinburgh the rate is 5% for those staying overnight in hotels, bed and breakfasts and self-catering facilities - capped at five nights.

Whereas in Liverpool, visitors to some hotels must pay a £2-per room overnight charge as part of a business-led scheme.

In March it was revealed the levy had so far raised about £10m .

The body behind the scheme pointed to the fund's success in helping to bring events such as the Labour Party Conference and the World Chess Championships to the city.

Hodgkinson, who owns Cobalt Studios in Ouseburn, said Newcastle was too quiet in the summer without its students and more needed to be done to encourage people to visit at the height of the tourist season.

She said the tax plans were "counterintuitive" and instead called for the mayor to put up taxes on empty buildings in the city to fund a boost of local tourism.

Noble, who runs the The Turks Head Inn in Rothbury, said she hated McGuinness's plans.

"Edinburgh is not Rothbury," she said. Noble said the village often had few tourists during the week and charging those customers more would just mean they headed elsewhere.

She said if McGuinness wanted to boost tourism to cities like Newcastle and Sunderland, then it should be tourists to those cities that paid the tax rather than rural visitors.

Andrew Golding, who runs the venue the Point in Sunderland, said tourists needed to be given more of a reason to visit the region before they were charged extra.

He said he welcomed plans to attract more large events to the area but that alone was not enough.

"A major event attracting thousands of people doesn't automatically mean those visitors spend money in local pubs, restaurants or grassroots music venues," he said.

Meanwhile Sam Booth, from the music venue Lubber Fiend in Newcastle, said they did not necessarily have an issue with taxing tourists if the money raised was spent properly.

"A fraction of the money they [the mayor and local authorities] spent on the Mercury Prize would guarantee our survival for 10 years," he said.

"And I would argue that we would have a much more tangible impact on local music and the local economy over that time."

In September four Reform UK-led councils in north-east England – Durham, Gateshead, South Tyneside and Sunderland – wrote to McGuinness arguing against her plans to introduce the tax.

They said: "Making the North East more expensive at the checkout risks driving visitors, spending and jobs to neighbouring regions."

Earlier this month, Durham County Council's deputy leader Darren Grimes called McGuinness a "megalomaniac" after she detailed the council pushback she had faced in a regional mayor's meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

In response McGuinness said the fee would be used to "fund major events" in the region.

"I guarantee this will create jobs and bring in thousands of tourists," she said.

She also said several other parts of the country were planning to bring in the levy which would mean they would have more money to promote tourism.

"I am not prepared to let the North East slip behind while others take our visitors," she said.

articles.title: Spider found in Mauritius like discovering 'hidden treasure'
articles.summary: The new species of trapdoor spider is discovered by scientists from Durrell working in Mauritius.
articles.body:
Scientists have said they are "completely stunned" after discovering a new species of spider.

A team from Jersey's Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust was working with partners on the Mauritian island of Ilot Vacoas when the arachnid was spotted along a stretch of rock along the coast in 2023.

The charity said the discovery was confirmed as a new species of trapdoor spider which was named the Mauritian tidal trapdoor spider (Idioctis marevallum).

Dr Max Tercel, the entomologist who found the spider, said it felt like uncovering a "hidden treasure".

Recalling the discovery, Tercel said he found the spider on "a stretch of coastal rock with sparse vegetation".

It was "not somewhere we expected to find something so remarkable", he said.

"It was dark by then and I was carefully searching through crevices with my head torch when, to my astonishment, I noticed a familiar pattern - a spider's legs extending from its burrow, something I'd only ever seen before in lush forests and grasslands," he said.

Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust said rather than digging its own burrow like other trapdoor spiders, the Mauritian tidal spider lived in tubes in coralline bedrock believed to be created by worms and molluscs thousands of years ago.

The spider seals the entrance with a trapdoor made from silk, sand and algae, the trust said, with its home completely submerged at high tide and repeatedly hit by waves.

Nik Cole, Mauritius country manager at Durrell, said the discovery was "incredibly exciting".

He said: "The thing I remember most is Max screaming at me to come over because he'd just seen a mygalomorph - a trapdoor spider.

"I couldn't believe something from the same group as tarantulas could be living in a place like this.

"I was up all night, holding my phone in the air trying to get a signal and searching for any evidence of a spider like this in Mauritius."

articles.title: Lucy Harrison death: Mum told UK police have 'no authority' in US
articles.summary: Jane Coates wrote to Cheshire police urging them to gather evidence into Lucy Harrison's killing.
articles.body:
The mother of a British woman who was shot and killed by her father in Texas has been told that police in the UK have "no lawful authority to intervene" as the family tries to find answers.

Lucy Harrison, 23, from Warrington was shot in the chest on 10 January 2025 in Prosper, Dallas - found by a UK coroner to be an unlawful killing.

However, no criminal case was brought against her father Kris Harrison, after a grand jury in Collin County declined to indict him.

Lucy's mother Jane Coates wrote to Cheshire Police urging them to "gather evidence" here locally, and then "liaise" with US authorities - but the force has responded and said it was "constrained" by law and jurisdiction.

In a letter to Coates, Deputy Chief Constable Mike Evans said: "Whilst we may share the family's concerns and understand their desire for further scrutiny, we have no lawful authority to intervene in decisions taken by those agencies."

Last month, Coates flew to Texas in a bid to meet the district attorney in Collin County and to call on him to reinstate the investigation but was told he would not speak to he r.

The grand jury had decided there was insufficient evidence to bring criminal charges after Kris Harrison said the Glock handgun discharged accidentally while he was showing it to his daughter.

In February, a coroner in England concluded Lucy had been unlawfully killed, finding that her father's actions amounted to gross negligence manslaughter under UK law.

Police in Texas have, however, said they would not reopen the investigation.

Evans said the force was "ultimately constrained by legal, jurisdictional and practical realities that significantly limit what any police force in England and Wales can do in relation to a death that occurred in the United States," he said.

Given the "unusual circumstances reported" of Lucy's death, a Senior Investigating Officer had been tasked with looking into the case.

That officer appointed a Family Liaison Officer and sought information from the relevant United States law enforcement agencies.

He said that despite the "clear jurisdictional limitations," the force's actions "reflected our recognition of the exceptional circumstances of the case and our commitment to providing whatever support and assistance was realistically available."

The family had argued that as Kris Harrison is a British citizen, a mechanism exists under certain circumstances, where those from the United Kingdom who commit murder or manslaughter, can be prosecuted before British courts.

In response, Evans said: "Even where jurisdiction may arguably exist in law, the practical ability to investigate and prosecute remains severely constrained when the suspect, witnesses, exhibits and evidential opportunities are all located overseas.

"No parent should have to endure the loss of a child in such tragic circumstances, and I fully appreciate that the passage of time does not diminish the family's need for answers or their determination to understand exactly what happened to Lucy," Evans added.

Coates' lawyer Radd Seiger, has since said the family had "serious concerns about the investigation and whether all the relevant evidence was properly gathered and considered.

Further information, including a recent download from Lucy's mobile phone, contained information which "we believe are relevant to the circumstances leading up to her death."

"We are not asking Cheshire Constabulary to take over an American investigation or to determine what happened in Texas.

Instead, he said they were asking the force "to obtain and examine relevant evidence which has not yet been properly investigated".

"The family have spent nearly two years trying to get answers about Lucy's death and justice for her.

"They are not prepared to accept that the investigation is complete simply because the American authorities have decided not to take the matter further," he added.

articles.title: Are Houthis using Russian satellites as Saudi Arabia fends off strikes?
articles.summary: Analysts say the seizure of state arsenals, external backing and extensive military evolution has helped the Houthis.
articles.body:
An investigation has revealed that Russian satellites are assisting the Iran-aligned Houthis to strike Saudi Arabia’s military and energy infrastructure, further upending global energy markets amid the US war on Iran.

Hostilities between the internationally recognised Yemeni government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, and the Houthis have been ongoing since July and escalated in September when the rebel group seized full control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast.

Last month, the Houthis also carried out a precision strike on pumping stations on Saudi Arabia’s most important oil pipeline, the East-West pipeline. An investigation by Geneva-based private firm AURORAH GeoSignal Intelligence revealed that Russian satellites had been surveying the region days in advance to gather intelligence about the pipeline.

With fighting for control of Yemen between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government continuing, how significant is Russia’s support to the Houthis? Why can’t Saudi Arabia, the most powerful of the Gulf states that is backed by the US, hold back a group of rebel fighters?

What did the investigation into the use of Russian satellites show?

As revealed by The Associated Press news agency this week, between July 1 and October 19, AURORAH Geosignal Intelligence examined 40 missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Houthis and, in every case, found a pattern of Russian government and military satellites observing the targeted areas both before and after the attacks.

Nawaf Obaid, founder of the geosignal intelligence firm, told Al Jazeera that by reconstructing Russia’s military reconnaissance architecture, the group had identified individual satellites, calculated their orbital trajectories and then established observation opportunities and correlated their activity with military developments across Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, the UAE and Yemen.

He said the satellites they identified include Russia’s Bars-M military mapping satellites, Persona optical reconnaissance satellites, Lotos-S1 electronic intelligence satellites, Pion-NKS maritime reconnaissance systems and Kondor-FKA radar-imaging satellites. They also examined the EKS/Tundra infrared early-warning constellation.

“The critical finding was not the presence of individual Russian satellites, but the sequencing and integration of their complementary intelligence capabilities,” he said.

Obaid also confirmed to Al Jazeera that based on the findings, “Russian military geospatial and signals intelligence has supported the Iranian-led intelligence architecture assisting Houthi operations in Yemen.”

He said the strongest operational example of this has been the Houthi offensive along Yemen’s western coast towards Bab al-Mandeb, where Russian-derived intelligence, Iranian command integration and local human intelligence all contributed to “the rapid deterioration of opposing Yemeni forces’ battlefield coordination”.

“We assess that this intelligence relationship is also relevant to Houthi missile and drone targeting against Saudi Arabia. Russian military reconnaissance provides capabilities far beyond ordinary commercial satellite imagery, particularly when optical, radar and electronic intelligence are integrated,” he said.

“The September attacks against Saudi Arabia’s East-West Petroline illustrate the sophistication of the targeting problem,” he said. That was when three pumping stations – PS8 at Afif, PS9 at Al-Dhekra and PS11 at Al-Mesba’ah – were struck within the pipeline’s “critical high-elevation western section”.

“Their selection reflected an understanding of the infrastructure’s engineering vulnerabilities and strategic importance,” he explained.

Brussels-based military analyst Elijah Magnier said AURORA’s findings don’t necessarily show the whole picture.

“Inability to intercept an intelligence transmission doesn’t establish who had access to the Russian satellite information, whether Russia deliberately shared it, or whether Iran obtained it independently,” he said, adding that for this, there are four possible scenarios.

“First, Russia could have deliberately shared information with Iran,” he said.

“The second is Iran obtained Russian satellite imagery through commercial channels… However, the Russian military’s reconnaissance imagery is generally not publicly accessible, so the commercial Russian imagery would not necessarily establish Russian government involvement,” he noted.

“The third is Iran obtained information through another intermediary, so a third party could theoretically have supplied the intelligence originated from the Russian system, and there is no currently publicly verified evidence establishing such an arrangement,” he added.

But Obaid highlighted that distinguishing a Russian-supported intelligence architecture from proof that a particular Russian satellite supplied the targeting data for an individual Houthi strike is essential.

“Our assessment establishes the wider intelligence relationship; attribution of specific satellite-derived intelligence to individual missile launches requires additional corroboration,” he said.

Three officials, including one from Saudi Arabia and another in the top ranks of the Houthis, as well as a private intelligence analyst, confirmed to The Associated Press that the Houthis and other Iranian allies have benefitted from Russian intelligence, as well as Chinese capabilities.

Last week, the Saudi Foreign Ministry’s deputy minister for public diplomacy, Rayed Krimly, told reporters that the Houthis receive intelligence from Russia and China.

“We do discuss these matters regularly with China and Russia, and we will continue to do so,” he had said.

How important is access to Russian satellites for Iran and the Houthis?

Russian officials have not yet commented on AURORAH’s findings, but in recent years, technological and military ties between Russia and Iran have deepened significantly, anchored by joint strategic agreements, space cooperation, and the exchange of defence technology.

Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst on Yemen at the International Crisis Group, said Moscow reportedly supporting Tehran’s allies like the Houthis is particularly significant because it would mean a shift in the trajectory of the Yemeni conflict.

“It is increasingly moving beyond its domestic dimensions and becoming intertwined with wider regional dynamics. Supporting the Houthis is no longer a matter of interest to Iran alone. We are now seeing other actors, particularly Russia, providing Iran with intelligence support and sophisticated weaponry, from which the Houthis are also benefitting,” he told Al Jazeera.

“The question is whether this support is being channelled directly to the Houthis or indirectly through Iran. I don’t think that distinction is important. The bottom line is that the Houthis are benefitting from increasingly diversified external support involving several countries,” he added.

But Nagi warned that Russian support to the Houthis has implications for both the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia.

“Russia’s role also extends into the diplomatic arena, where Moscow has taken positions at the United Nations Security Council opposing stronger international action against the Houthis. Taken together, these developments point to a broader expansion of Russian engagement with the group,” he added.

Where have the Houthis struck in Saudi Arabia?

Yemen’s Houthis have attacked multiple locations across Saudi Arabia, spanning from the eastern and western coasts to the capital and southern regions, since fighting escalated over the summer.

In a statement on X on Friday, Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed attacks have hit vital commercial and military infrastructure, which spanned Saudi Arabia from its east and west coasts to Riyadh and the southern region of Najran.

Saree said the Houthis targeted the Ras Tanura oil refinery with a ballistic missile, an Aramco facility in Abqaiq with a missile, King Khalid International airport in Riyadh with multiple missiles, King Fahd International airport in Dammam with a drone, the Rabigh oil refinery with a ballistic missile and a Saudi military headquarters in the Najran region.

There has, however, been no independent corroboration of these specific claims.

However, Houthi attacks generally have resulted in multiple deaths and injuries in Saudi Arabia. A severe strike on King Khalid International airport in Riyadh earlier this month killed at least 12 people and injured 300, according to Saudi officials. The attacks led to the airport’s temporary closure, forcing the postponement of Saudi Arabia’s flagship investment conference until 2027 and disrupting travel plans for thousands of passengers.

The airport has since reopened, and flights resumed on Sunday with the Houthis warning travellers to avoid the facility, calling it a “military target”.

An October 21 attack on King Fahd International airport in Dammam also killed two people and wounded eight.

Since seizing Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, and swaths of northwest Yemen in 2014, the Houthis have demanded to be recognised as the legitimate governing authority in Yemen.

After taking the capital and state institutions, the Houthis gained access to large arsenals belonging to the Yemeni military and formed an alliance with forces loyal to former President Ali Abdullah Saleh.

The internationally recognised government decamped to Aden.

Once regarded as an armed group without many resources, analysts say this has changed since the Houthis seized Yemen state arsenals, received external backing from Iran, and evolved their military capabilities.

Saj Ahmad, chief analyst at StrategicAero Research, told Al Jazeera that besides learning the art of weapons assembly, the Houthis have scoured international black markets for components and carried out many military engagements to unearth a clandestine, but robust, market for sales, too.

“So while the Houthis have been expending their cache of weapons, they have been developing and expanding too – and we have seen that with their long-range missile attacks as far away as Israel – so targeting high-value targets in Saudi Arabia in contrast is very easy pickings for them,” he said.

When a truce between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition took effect in 2022 and continued until earlier this year, many within the Yemeni government expected it to pave the way for a political settlement, Nagi said.

“The Houthis, meanwhile, were preparing for the possibility that the conflict would resume. They used the relative lull to strengthen their military position. The extent of that preparation has become evident over the past few weeks. Their forces have demonstrated considerable military readiness, enabling them to advance across several areas and inflict significant setbacks on Yemeni government forces,” he said.

According to Magnier, the Houthis’ sophisticated missile propulsion and guidance technology remains heavily dependent on foreign expertise, however.

The Houthis receive substantial backing, training and weaponry from Iran. This includes Iranian-origin and-derived ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and one-way attack drones – such as the Palestine-2 and Toufan systems – although Iran officially denies supplying them.

Besides Iran, Magnier said Iran’s ally in Lebanon, Hezbollah, has also contributed with military training and organisational experience. “All the experience gathered from fighting Israel was transformed and offered to Ansar Allah [the name the Houthis are also known by] in Yemen,” he said.

“The cooperation has also extended to Iraqi armed groups, with the exchange involving military personnel and again operational experience in a vast area,” he added.

“This combination [of domestic expansion and foreign dependence] helps explain why years of Saudi-led military operation, followed by American and Israeli strikes, have failed to eliminate its military capability,” he added.

How has Saudi Arabia struck back at the Houthis?

The Saudi-led coalition has retaliated against Houthi targets in Yemen through air attacks and military operations.

On Friday, the coalition in Yemen reported that it intercepted a drone launched by the Houthis towards Saudi Arabia’s Mecca region.

The drone was “intercepted and destroyed” on Friday morning, coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said in a social media post. It was also reported that a missile aimed at western Saudi Arabia was earlier brought down, as hostilities between the Riyadh-backed Yemen government and Iran-backed Houthis continue to escalate.

On Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards the kingdom’s eastern region. It later said two ballistic missiles launched towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh, were also intercepted and destroyed.

Al-Malki reported early on Friday that the coalition’s air defences intercepted and destroyed a Houthi cruise missile which had targeted western Saudi Arabia.

Al-Maliki said on Monday its forces also destroyed four ballistic missile launchers and five tunnels used by the Houthis to store missiles.

In a post on X, he had said coalition forces attacked a missile depot, adding that the operation “focused on cutting off Houthi militia supply lines between areas under their control”.

The operation also targeted Houthi “fortifications, gatherings of their members, and their military equipment along the front lines inside Yemen”.

Al-Maliki said on Monday that Saudi air defences “intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh”.

This month, Yemen’s government forces launched the “Operation Yemen Dawn” counteroffensive, aimed at recapturing territory held by the Houthis.

On Sunday, the Saudi-led military coalition said air defences intercepted at least 10 ballistic missiles.

The kingdom’s civil defence agency said two people were injured in the south by falling debris, and reported damage to several buildings and vehicles.

Why are the Saudis struggling to contain the Houthis?

While high-level diplomatic talks such as recent meetings in Tehran involving Saudi and Iranian officials have aimed to de-escalate tensions, analysts say the Houthis are actively testing the limits of Saudi military restraint and air defence capabilities, transforming the Yemeni conflict into a wider national security test for Riyadh.

According to Magnier, the Saudis have been struggling because “nobody wins a war by air bombing.”

“The air bombing helps for the ground forces to capitalise on what the air force is doing and opens the road for the ground forces. If the ground forces are not sufficiently motivated to advance and offer sacrifices and accept large losses, then there is no point in wondering why the Saudis are struggling,” he said.

Crisis group’s Nagi shared a similar view. He added that the Saudi-backed Yemeni government camp has also remained fragmented, poorly organised and militarily unprepared.

“There was an expectation that quick fixes, particularly intensified air strikes, could produce rapid gains. But the government and its allies had not developed the military capabilities or organisation necessary to sustain a confrontation with the Houthis,” he said.

According to analyst Saj Ahmad, despite the billions spent on US and European weapons, the Saudis have failed to make effective use of their military capabilities.

“The Houthis have learned a great deal from Iran’s military strategists as well as those militias in and across Iraq that battled US troops for years after the fall of Saddam Hussein. And in that intervening period, the Saudi regime has made big weapon buys but has little skill in how to use or deploy them and has even less capability to effectively combat a guerrilla group like the Houthis,” he said.

“With Riyadh under siege, I would not be surprised if the Saudis eventually leave this combat zone, like the UAE did,” he added.
