articles.title: Dead dolphins, naval mines: Russia-Ukraine war destroys the Black Sea
articles.summary: Conflict devastates Black Sea marine life, killing more than 120,000 dolphins and causing ecological damage.
articles.body:
Kyiv, Ukraine – Fishers and poachers along the Black Sea coast often find suffocated dolphins entangled in their nets

They release them by cutting off their fins and dropping them in the sea. Their bodies, with net marks on their skin, are often washed ashore.

Fishing and poaching in littoral Black Sea nations plummeted because of Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion, as Moscow strove to occupy all of Ukraine’s Black Sea coast.

It failed – but the ongoing hostilities have been killing “hundreds times more” bottlenose and short-beaked dolphins and harbour porpoises, according to Ivan Rusev, head researcher at the Tuzly Lagoons national park in southern Ukraine.

In 2022 alone, some 50,000 dolphins died this way, and by 2026, the number exceeded 120,000, or one in four cetaceans in the Black Sea, Rusev told Al Jazeera.

Dolphins are apex predators, and their decimation further ruins the Black Sea’s ecosystem already affected by chemicals from munitions, spills of oil, fuel and vegetable oils from dozens of sunk or damaged warships, tankers and freighters.

Many dead dolphins still have their fins, but look starved.

Explosions, launches of cruise missiles from warships, and military sonar systems confuse them, deafening their primary survival tool, echolocation, and making them unable to navigate, communicate and hunt.

“If a dolphin can’t fish, it loses weight fast,” said Rusev, whose park covers 280 square kilometres (108 square miles) of salty lagoons that serve as a stopover and breeding site for migratory birds.

The dolphins switch to consuming their blubber that has already accumulated pollutants from wastewater, agricultural runoff, microplastics and antibiotics.

The self-poisoning incapacitates their immune system, and they succumb to lethal respiratory tract infections caused by the so-called morbillivirus.

The Black Sea is one of the world’s youngest – some scholars hypothesise that it was a freshwater lake until about eight millennia ago, when the Bosporus Strait burst open, causing what may have been the biblical Great Flood.

The sea’s waters lack oxygen and support no fauna or flora below 50 to 100 metres.

The chronic environmental damage from the war was aggravated by another shock: the 2023 destruction of the giant Kakhovka dam on the Dnipro River, releasing most of its 18 cubic kilometres (4.3 cubic miles) of water contaminated with fertiliser runoff, heavy metals and machine oil.

Fish species such as mullet and bluefish have become scarce, even though fishing in Black Sea nations has been affected by restrictions, bans and naval mines that were spotted near Istanbul.

The changes inevitably affect the dolphins.

“With dolphins at the top of the food chain, everything from zooplankton to fish reaches them,” Rusev said.

Environmentalists from other Black Sea nations – Bulgaria, Romania, Turkiye – also reported a spike in dolphin deaths, even though the cause of their death couldn’t always be established.

“Most of the stranded dead cetaceans are usually in an advanced state of decomposition, making detection of net marks and other marks almost impossible,” Dimitar Popov of Green Balkans, Bulgaria’s oldest nature conservation group, told Al Jazeera.

He agrees with Rusev that “sonar systems of warships and submarines definitely affect cetaceans and their echolocation and hearing abilities”.

Meanwhile, Russian environmental monitors blamed the dolphin deaths on “parasites” and “virus infections” without any further explanation.

And even though only a tiny percentage of dead dolphins are washed ashore, their appearance horrifies Ukrainians already unnerved by nearly daily drone and missile attacks.

In August, Tetiana Smolchenko enjoyed a seaside stroll with her eight-year-old son Oleh in the southern city of Odesa – until the child spotted an emaciated, decaying dolphin.

“I nearly threw up,” the 33-year-old, whose husband serves in the military and whose apartment building has been damaged by a Russian drone twice, told Al Jazeera.

“We’re so used to human deaths now, but seeing these creatures die because of the war is no less horrifying,” she said. “We both wept.”

What looks like a military triumph could become a heavy blow to the marine ecosystem.

Since 2022, Ukrainian sea and airborne drones have sunk two submarines and three dozen Russian warships, including the Black Sea Fleet’s flagship, the Moskva (Moscow) guided missile cruiser.

They were all loaded with toxic fuel and other chemicals.

Even though Ukrainian drone operators attacking Russian “shadow fleet” tankers are instructed to specifically target their engines, oil and fuel spills continue to happen.

Oil molecules form a film that coats seaweed, poisoning molluscs and fish, especially sturgeons that die in droves.

Every explosion deafens and kills fish, and the sound, coupled with flying drones, startles birds migrating back and forth between Northern Europe and the Middle East.

“And when a bird can’t find enough food, doesn’t have ‘fuel,’ it can’t reach the destination where it winters or nests,” Rusev said. “It will affect the number of certain bird populations for years.”

Startled by the blasts, flamingoes, who only started nesting in his park years ago, are leaving their hatches, and seagulls immediately eat the eggs, he said.

The war’s only silver lining for wild nature around the sea is that the number of boars, roes, foxes, jackals, hares and badgers has risen because hunting and poaching nearly stopped, he said.

And the ecosystem’s post-war recovery is going to be uneven.

While the number of insects and small mammals should return to normal within years, the dolphin population’s recovery will take decades.

“We estimate that it would take 30 to 50 years to renew the population of cetaceans, so that the sea ecosystem becomes more or less normal,” Rusev said.

articles.title: How man's Halloween house display has become bittersweet tradition
articles.summary: Dave Barron, 61, from Bramhall, says his Halloween displays raise money for a charity and are a tribute to his late wife.
articles.body:
As people up and down the country look forward to celebrating Halloween this evening, one Greater Manchester man takes the festivities further than most.

Dave Barron, 61, from Bramhall, in Greater Manchester, has been decorating his home for Halloween every year since 2011, and has been preparing this year's Back to the Future-themed display since May.

Dave's efforts are all a tribute to his late wife, Catherine. Accepting donations from Halloween visitors, he has raised more than £55,000 for the Macmillan cancer charity, which cared for Catherine before she died in 2020.

"Halloween is emotional for me," Dave said. "I miss Catherine tremendously. She'd think I'm an absolute lunatic, but she was always a big part of it and I think she'd be really proud."

"I have been working on this year's Halloween display since May," he said. "And it does cost me a bit.

"But It's a small price to pay if it helps people who are suffering with cancer."

"Within the last decade it's just got it bigger and bigger and bigger," Dave said of his Halloween extravaganzas."

Dave put on a Doctor Who-themed display last year, but said this year's had been the most challenging project yet.

"This has probably been our most ambitious challenge in all the years we've done it," he said.

"I thought building a Dalek last year was bad enough, but the car we built this year has got that many angles and twists and turns on it.

"But we've got there. We started around end of May and we've been working on it pretty much ever since, weather-permitting."

Dave has been helped by his 27-year-old daughter Sarah and other family members and friends.

He also hands out more than 500 sweets, donated by his local Tesco, during each event.

"There's so many people, from the timber company, to the tyre company, to a friend who makes our banners, to everyone else who has chipped in, lending us instruments, donating costumes," he said.

Dave said he was particularly touched when a stranger responded to his Facebook appeal looking for a 1981 DeLorean DMC-12.

"I wanted to take measurements to make it as realistic as possible, so we could build it to size," Dave said.

"A lady wrote back to me almost instantly and she said my husband has one, he's out in it at the moment.

"He offered to come to our house from his home in Poynton and left the car with us for the day.

"It's people stepping in like that that shows you how far community can stretch."

Dave also said he was hoping to be paid another visit from Salford comedian, actor and singer Jason Manford, who has become a regular attendee over the years.

"They are aiming to come this year," Dave said. "They have their own party and they tend to come a little bit later on."

Dave said while his displays were to honour his wife's legacy, he felt proud to be able to know he was helping others.

"When I sit back and I look at what we've done, it actually is very, very emotional," he added.

articles.title: Manhunt launched after California Spirit Halloween shooting leaves 1 dead, 6 injured
articles.summary: A manhunt is underway for a shooter who killed one person and injured six in a Spirit Halloween store on Friday night, police in Fairfield, California said.
articles.body: A manhunt is underway for a shooter who killed one person and injured six in a Spirit Halloween store on Friday night, police in Fairfield, California said. At least three victims are “currently in critical condition,” Fairfield Police Department Chief Dan Marshall told a news conference about the incident at the Solano Town Center mall, which took place at around 8:30 p.m. local time (5:30 p.m. ET) “Our thoughts and prayers are with the families of the victims of this heartbreaking incident,” he said, adding that all of the victims had been taken to a nearby hospital. No further information was provided about those shot. Detectives were “diligently working to identify the suspect or suspects responsible for this horrific shooting,” Marshall said. David Bernal told NBC News affiliate KCRA that his wife was in the store when the shooter opened fire but she had managed to escape with several other people through an emergency exit. “She’s at home right now, still in shock,” he said, adding that she told him she heard “five big bangs, big ones, like loud.” He added that she started running and made her way “out from the one of the exits on the other side of the mall.” The incident came hours after another person was shot dead inside a Spirit Halloween store in Madison Heights, Michigan. “A 21-year-old Detroit resident sustained serious injuries and was transported to a local hospital,” the Madison Heights Police Department said in a news release. He later “succumbed to those injuries,” the release said. The alleged shooter, a 21-year-old man, “sustained non life threatening injuries after being assaulted by several bystanders as officers took him into custody,” police said, adding that he was taken to hospital. “Based on the evidence gained thus far, investigators anticipate seeking criminal charges in this case,” the release said. The incidents do not appear to be connected.

articles.title: Daylight saving time ends Sunday. Here’s what to know as clocks ‘fall back’
articles.summary: Clocks across much of the United States will fall back once again Sunday as daylight saving time comes to an end.
articles.body: Clocks across much of the United States will fall back once again Sunday as daylight saving time comes to an end. Congress and some states have tried multiple times this decade to get rid of the twice-yearly exercise but to no avail. President Donald Trump has expressed support for ending the time changes, arguing that permanent daylight saving time would allow for more daylight to parallel daytime habits while shrinking after-hours activity, including crime. But many health and sleep experts argue against it, citing risks to health and safety. Here is what to know as we prepare to spin our clocks back Sunday — or let our cellphones do it instantly. When does daylight saving time end? Daylight saving time started at 2 a.m. March 8 and ends at 2 a.m. Sunday. Unlike in the spring, when we lose an hour and the clocks skip the 2 o’clock hour entirely, we will gain an extra hour Sunday, with clocks jumping from 1:59 a.m. back to 1 a.m. The sun will also start setting earlier across the United States as we head into the late fall and winter. The extra hour doesn’t necessarily mean more revelry on Halloween night: While some jurisdictions allow bars to serve last call according to Sunday’s updated time, California rules say bars must stop serving alcohol two hours past midnight, regardless of 1 a.m.’s repeat. How long will standard time last? Standard time across the United States will remain, as will earlier sunsets and darker evenings, until spring rolls around and daylight saving time starts once again on March 14. Daylight saving time will end next year on Nov. 7. The standardized start and end dates have been changed throughout the years, but since 2007, daylight saving time has started the second Sunday in March and ended the first Sunday in November, according to the Astronomical Applications Department of the U.S. Naval Observatory. Why do we observe daylight saving time? The practice, established by the Standard Time Act in 1918, according to the Astronomical Applications Department, is an effort to extend the daylight hours we have in the summertime by pushing off sunset an extra hour. Daylight saving time, a contested idea after it was passed, was quickly repealed in 1919, becoming a local matter. It was re-enacted during the early days of World War II and observed from 1942 to 1945, according to the department. After the war, the implementation of daylight saving time varied from state to state until the Uniform Time Act was passed in 1966, standardizing the dates of daylight saving time but allowing local exemptions if states or localities didn’t want to participate. President Richard Nixon briefly moved the nation to year-round daylight saving time in 1974, but the extended morning darkness was widely panned and blamed for incidents of students being struck by vehicles. Congress subsequently reversed his time changes after Nixon resigned later that year. Which states don’t observe? Hawaii and most of Arizona don’t observe daylight saving time and therefore don’t change their clocks twice a year, according to the Astronomical Applications Department. The U.S. territories of American Samoa, Guam, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands and the Northern Mariana Islands also observe permanent standard time, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. Do other countries do this? Most countries observe some version of “summer time,” according to the department, not all of them on the same schedule as the United States. Most of the countries in the Northern Hemisphere that observe daylight saving time are in Europe and North America. Some Southern Hemisphere countries also observe some version of daylight saving time, but below the equator, the seasons are swapped, so the start and end dates of their “summer time” are reversed from ours. According to the Pew Research Center, only about a third of all countries observe daylight saving time. About half of all countries observed it at one point but no longer do. What recent efforts have been made to end the practice? Almost all states have considered legislation to stay on standard or daylight saving time, and 19 states have passed bills or resolutions to implement it year-round in the last seven years, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. But because federal law doesn’t allow for year-round daylight saving time, the states would have to wait for Congress to pass a bill to make the change. The Senate passed the Sunshine Protection Act in 2022, which would make daylight saving time permanent year-round, but the bill didn’t advance in the House. A version of the bill introduced in the House in January 2025 stalled in the Senate in summer. In early October, Trump in a post on Truth Social urged Senate Republicans to “get moving” on the bill, saying the clock changing process “costs our Country a fortune, is bad for Crime, stress on people, Sports, and just about everything else you can imagine.” What do health experts say? Some studies suggest that observing daylight saving time year-round could reduce the number of traffic accidents and the amount of crime. But many health and sleep researchers aren’t in favor of permanent daylight saving time, namely because of the potential hazards of dark mornings, which would mean more children walking or driving to school in the dark. Sleep experts prefer the back-and-forth of the clocks to permanent daylight saving time, and point to the increased risks of health problems when clocks aren’t closely aligned with the sun.

articles.title: Flights diverted after drones flown near airport
articles.summary: Jersey Airport says three flights were diverted because of "unauthorised drone activity".
articles.body:
Flights were diverted and cancelled due to "unauthorised drone activity" near an airport.

Jersey Airport said three flights were diverted back to the UK because of drones flying in the airport's restricted airspace on Friday evening.

States of Jersey Police said it responded to the incident with the Honorary Police, Channel Islands Air Search, Government of Jersey colleagues and Ports of Jersey staff.

Searches were carried out across several areas in the west of the island but no drone operator has yet been identified.

Flights due to arrive from London Gatwick, London Heathrow and Southampton were diverted. The Gatwick flight eventually arrived but the services from Heathrow and Southampton were cancelled.

A spokesperson for Jersey Police said: "We should not underestimate the impact that this had on travelling passengers, staff at the airport and the wider community.

"The reported drone activity occurred within restricted airspace and active flight paths, resulting in significant disruption to airport operations and passengers.

"Three inbound aircraft were initially diverted. One of the three was ultimately able to land safely in Jersey at around 23:45 GMT.

" Passengers experienced considerable delays and inconvenience while agencies worked to ensure the safety of aircraft, passengers and crew.

The police are particularly keen to hear from anyone who was in the St Peter, La Pulente, Watersplash, El Tico, L'Etacq, Jubilee Hill or surrounding areas and saw any drone activity.

articles.title: Lebanon charges 13 over confiscated Hezbollah explosives
articles.summary: Group calls charges ‘unjust’, says weapons were meant to be used against Israeli forces in south Lebanon.
articles.body:
A Lebanese military court has charged 13 people it says are linked to Hezbollah with trafficking explosives , amid growing pressure on the Iran-backed group to disarm .

The individuals were charged on Friday with offences including possessing weapons, undermining state security and forming illegal associations, Lebanese state media reported.

The charges stem from the seizure earlier this month of a truck transporting explosives at Dahr al-Baydar checkpoint, which links the capital, Beirut, to the eastern Bekaa Valley.

The vehicle had been carrying 780kg (1,720 pounds) of explosives, including 250kg (550 pounds) of TNT and 250kg (550 pounds) of C-4 plastic explosives, according to judicial officials.

Two people were arrested during the seizure, while the 11 others charged remain at large. Five have been identified only by nicknames because their real names are unknown.

Hezbollah has acknowledged owning the seized explosives, saying they were intended for use against Israel, which continues to occupy large parts of southern Lebanon. It said it had asked Lebanese authorities to return the shipment and release the two detainees, calling the charges against them “unjust”.

Those charged “did not undermine the security or integrity of the state, but rather confronted the Israeli enemy that threatens Lebanon’s existence,” said Hezbollah Member of Parliament Hussein Hajj Hassan.

Hezbollah’s political opponents fear that smuggled explosives will be turned against the group’s detractors, although investigators have not established that the seized shipment was intended for such an attack.

The case comes as pressure mounts on Hezbollah , which has fought two successive wars with Israel and faces a push from authorities in Beirut, to disarm its military wing.

In June, Lebanon and Israel signed a framework agreement which envisaged Israel’s gradual withdrawal from the areas it occupies in southern Lebanon, tied to Hezbollah’s disarmament, as well as the deployment of the Lebanese army to the south.

But Hezbollah has repeatedly rejected calls to disarm, and the group’s chief, Naim Qassem, has dismissed the Lebanon-Israel agreement as “null and void”.

Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has promised state authorities “will deal with weapons outside the legal framework with the required firmness”.

Despite its recent framework agreement, Israel has continued carrying out attacks in southern Lebanon and systematically demolishing homes and infrastructure in dozens of villages it occupies.

articles.title: Rival US and Russian resolutions on Western Sahara fail at UN
articles.summary: UN Security Council rejected the competing proposals, leaving the peacekeeping mission without an approved extension.
articles.body:
The United Nations peacekeeping mission in the disputed Western Sahara faces an uncertain future after competing United States and Russian resolutions failed at the UN Security Council.

Russia vetoed the US-backed proposal on Friday, despite support from 11 members of the 15-member council.

A rival Russian draft then failed to secure the nine votes needed for adoption.

The mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) is due to expire on Saturday unless the council reaches a last-minute agreement.

Western Sahara is a former Spanish colony in northwest Africa. Morocco considers the territory its own while the Algeria-backed Polisario Front seeks to establish an independent state called the Sahrawi Republic.

The UN established MINURSO in 1991 to monitor a ceasefire and prepare a referendum on the territory’s future, but disagreements over who could vote have prevented it from taking place.

The US draft would have extended the mission for a year while removing “referendum” from its name and making Morocco’s autonomy proposal the only basis for further talks.

Under that plan, the territory would manage its internal affairs but remain under Moroccan sovereignty.

The council had already made the proposal a basis for negotiations last year.

US Ambassador Mike Waltz told the council in New York on Friday that the referendum had been stalled for decades.

Russia’s UN ambassador, Vassily Nebenzia, said at the same meeting that Moscow opposed the draft because it favoured one side.

Russia instead proposed renewing the existing mission without those changes.

Morocco’s royal palace welcomed the failure to renew MINURSO, saying on Friday that UN personnel and equipment should leave the territory.

Sidi Omar, the Polisario Front’s representative at the UN, told reporters on Friday that he welcomed Russia’s veto because the US proposal would undermine Sahrawi self-determination.

Low-level fighting has continued since Polisario said it was resuming armed struggle in 2020.

articles.title: U.K. PM Andy Burnham open to apologizing for slave trade but rules out financial reparations
articles.summary: U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that he is open to am apology for his country’s role in the slave trade, but ruled out financial reparations.
articles.body: LONDON — British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that he is open to a formal apology for his country’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, but ruled out financial reparations as King Charles III continued his tour of the Caribbean. Burnham’s comments show a marked shift in stance for the U.K., which has consistently rejected demands for either an apology or reparations. They came as he is due to attend the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda next week. Charles, as head of the “family of nations,” will preside over the event. “We are offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade,” Burnham wrote in an op-ed in The Guardian newspaper in an article published Friday. “Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them.” But Burnham ruled out financial reparations, saying the British people of today who “played no personal part” in the slave trade could not be held liable. The transatlantic trade in enslaved people was central to European colonialism and the growth of the British Empire, as millions of Africans were trafficked to the Americas to grow and harvest cash crops, while being subjected to violence, torture, sexual abuse and the denial of basic human rights. Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, said on X that he welcomed the prime minister’s openness to a formal apology. Jamaica’s prime minister, Andrew Holness, also took to X where he wrote: “Open-minded dialogue is always a good place to start addressing difficult issues.” Jamaica recently took its case for reparations to Charles, and the case has since been referred to the United Kingdom’s highest court of appeal. Caribbean nations had urged British to acknowledge its role in the salve trade ahead of Charles’ visit to the Bahamas and Guyana last week. Charles visited Clifford Park last week where in 1973 he granted The Bahamas independence after 300 years of British rule. Members of The Bahamas’ Rastafarian community and others lined a nearby road to protest. “Pay us what you owe us!” one woman cried out. “I stand in memory of the horrors and the atrocities committed against Black people.” In his first public remarks on the island nation, Charles said: “It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present.”

articles.title: Cities fearing Halloween mayhem put teens on notice, announce curfews and crackdowns after violent takeovers
articles.summary: Oak Park, Illinois, and other cities are enforcing Halloween curfews and boosting police patrols after teen takeovers sparked fights and arrests.
articles.body: Cities across the country are putting teens on notice for Halloween weekend, rolling out curfews and crackdowns to head off the kind of chaos that unfolds during so-called teen takeovers. From the Jersey Shore to suburban Atlanta, officials are setting curfews for teenagers and adding police patrols, many of them in places still reeling from takeovers that drew hundreds of teens and ended in fights and arrests. In Oak Park, Illinois, the chief of police wrote that her agency is trying to prevent a similar Halloween teen takeover last year from happening again. INSIDE THE TEEN TAKEOVERS THREATENING TO EXPLODE THIS SUMMER AS CITIES REMAIN ON EDGE: 'VERY WORRIED' Last Halloween, an estimated 500 teens swarmed downtown Oak Park, where fights and gunshots erupted and police called in help from six neighboring agencies, according to a department memo. Oak Park Chief of Police Shatonya Johnson said the agency will be increasing the amount of officers on shift during Halloween, as well as several more measures aimed at preventing another teen takeover. CHICAGO MAYOR WARNS OF ‘TEEN TREND’ AFTER TAKEOVER CHAOS, VIOLENCE CONCERNS GROW Adults in the Hyde Park neighborhood of Chicago are taking matters into their own hands and plan to show out en masse on the streets to prevent large gatherings by teenagers. The group, called CollaBOOration, was established after a series of large Halloween gatherings from 2016 to 2019 where teen takeovers turned violent, according to Block Club Chicago. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X "What we’re really trying to do is establish a critical mass on the street, possibly before the Halloween festivities even start," the group's founder Bennie Currie said. "So when these large gatherings happen, like we’ve seen every year, we will already have taken over 53rd Street … we’ll be walking up and down in orange shirts and keeping in contact with one another." SEND US A TIP After 7 p.m. on Halloween, those under 16 in Covington, Georgia will be required to go home or have an adult with them if they're in the city's downtown area, which is outside Atlanta, according to CBS News. According to News 12, the Long Branch, New Jersey, police department plans to strictly enforce a Halloween curfew for those under 17 on Oct. 31, which runs from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST The curfew was set in response to hundreds of people gathering for a teen takeover in May, resulting in fights breaking out and six arrests. They're calling because there's a fight in a schoolyard. They're calling because they can't find their kid. There's so many different things that people are calling the police for, and then you factor in this desire to have these large crowds of teenagers take over and, again, get it on social media," Smith said.

articles.title: Civilians from war-ravaged Oleshky arrive in Belarus during Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire
articles.summary: Four planes carrying residents evacuated from the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky have landed in Belarus, the country’s state ​news agency and a senior Ukrainian official said Saturday.
articles.body: Four planes carrying residents evacuated from the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky have landed in Belarus, the country’s state ​news agency and a senior Ukrainian official said Saturday. Hundreds of starving and exhausted ‌residents left the town of Oleshky on Friday during a local ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump, the first of its kind and the longest humanitarian pause in the war, which is nearing its fifth year. “The ​last, fourth plane landed in Gomel,” said David Arakhamia, a top Ukrainian ​peace negotiator and close ally of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. “In a few ⁠hours, all Ukrainian citizens evacuated from Oleshky together with a Ukrainian delegation will be ​on Ukrainian territory.” Belarus’ Belta news agency later reported that a convoy of buses carrying the residents had ​departed from the airport in Gomel, in southeastern Belarus near the border with Ukraine. The evacuees leaving for Ukraine had to take a complicated route to leave Oleshky as the frontline runs just ​a few miles away. They first travelled by bus via Crimea to the Russian town ​of Anapa before flying to Belarus from where they will continue to Ukraine via a border ‌crossing, ⁠Belta reported. The local ceasefire in Oleshky was reached thanks to mediation efforts by first lady Melania Trump and with the involvement of Pope Leo XIV. The ceasefire has been holding since Tuesday without violations, according to both Ukrainian and Russian officials. It has allowed them ​to de-mine the roads ​and bring food, ⁠medicines and other supplies into the town. Supply routes to Oleshky were disrupted by fighting and drones. According to some residents, food ​deliveries were stopped in May, pushing hundreds of people into starvation. It ​was not ⁠immediately clear how many people decided to leave Oleshky and how many opted to stay in the town. Oleshky residents had options to travel to Russia or to return ⁠to ​Ukraine. Ukrainian officials have said around 1,700 people remained in ​Oleshky from a pre-war population of about 24,000. According to several residents interviewed by Reuters, many of those ​were elderly or ill.

articles.title: How Ambani’s Jio became India’s second-largest company
articles.summary: Jio makes India’s largest-ever stock market debut, raising $3.2bn in IPO.
articles.body:
New Delhi, India – This week, Mumbai, India’s financial capital, was the site of a splashy display by Asia’s richest man, Mukesh Ambani, with DJ sets, a drone show and a jam session with popular Indian singers.

The festivities marked India’s largest-ever initial public offering (IPO), as Ambani’s Jio Platforms raised $3.2bn in its stock market debut.

The telecoms-to-digital company’s shares surged by a whopping 21 percent on Wednesday, valuing the company at $131.5bn and making it the country’s second most valuable, only behind its parent, Ambani’s Reliance Industries.

The Ambani family’s Jio Platforms counts global tech giants Meta and Google among its major shareholders, following their multibillion-dollar investments in the company in 2020 – and serves more than 530 million customers.

“Jio may not be visible. But it pulses through every digital dream of India,” said Anant Ambani, the family’s youngest son, who is an additional director on the company’s board, at the celebratory event. “Today, Jio is shared with India.”

So, how did Ambani’s Jio disrupt one of the world’s most competitive telecoms markets – and in the process, help consolidate it into what some observers describe as an oligopoly?

Mukesh Ambani is the richest man in Asia, according to Forbes magazine, with a net worth of $80bn.

In the world’s most populous country – with more than one billion people – some say it is no exaggeration to call India “Ambani’s world”.

Since inheriting Reliance Industries from his father, Mukesh Ambani, 69, has expanded the conglomerate far beyond its textile and petrochemical roots.

From food and clothes to fuel, the internet and streaming, the reach of the Ambani family’s business empire extends into nearly every facet of daily life in India.

In October, United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio travelled to India for a two-day visit, during which he toured the Jamnagar refinery complex in Gujarat, owned by Ambani’s Reliance Industries. Rubio did not visit New Delhi on that trip and officials were angered by suggestions that ministers should travel to see him instead.

How did Jio become India’s largest telecoms operator?

In 2016, while American consumers were paying an average of about $7 per gigabyte of mobile data, Reliance entered the scene in India with Jio, upending one of the biggest telecommunication markets by size, by offering data free for months.

Jio crossed 100 million subscribers in its first 170 days in business, a milestone described at the time as the fastest achieved by a mobile operator globally. Those days were notable for the long queues in front of pop-up tents in Indian cities, giving away SIM cards.

But entry barriers into India’s then diverse telecom market were also high. Jio’s entry required a total investment commitment of nearly $22.48bn in September 2016, spent on spectrum acquisition, network infrastructure and fibre backhaul.

Backed by Reliance’s deep pockets, Jio’s arrival fundamentally changed India’s telecoms market – prepping itself to absorb initial losses in operations in exchange for the prize of accumulating millions of customers.

Competitors were forced to slash their prices sharply, consumption surged and millions of Indians began accessing the internet on their smartphones.

In just three years, Jio had become India’s largest telecom operator by subscriber numbers. In the coming years, Ambani expanded Jio into a digital ecosystem including JioCinema and entertainment for streaming and sporting events, and JioCloud for cloud storage and digital services.

Since 2016, when Jio was launched, Ambani’s fortune has grown nearly 3.8 times – with increase of approximately $60bn.

Jio’s entry triggered a 42.8 percent decline in India’s average telecom revenues per subscriber, from nearly $1.32 in 2016 to $0.75 in 2019, according to a research paper published in ScienceDirect.

The researchers believe the scale of this price decline was unprecedented and left India with a highly concentrated telecom market.

In the meantime, seven of the 10 incumbent operators exited the market either due to bankruptcy or merger, notably Aircel, Videocon, Telenor India, Tata Teleservices and Reliance Communications.

Reliance Communications, founded by Anil Ambani, Mukesh’s younger brother, suffered severe financial losses and filed for bankruptcy in 2019. The brothers, once joint heirs to their father’s business empire, have had a long and bitter falling-out over the division of the Reliance conglomerate following his death in 2002, with their rivalry playing out for years.

Today, Jio and Airtel have strengthened their positions, while Vodafone Idea continues to face financial difficulties. These three operators control more than 92 percent of India’s telecoms market.

Researchers found that while consumers benefitted from cheap services during the price war, those benefits declined after the market reconsolidated.

In July 2024, Jio introduced price increases of approximately 12 to 25 percent across plans and other telecom operators followed suit, also raising tariffs substantially.

In its IPO disclosures, Jio has noted that further tariff increases may not necessarily translate into higher revenues because consumers could downgrade plans or switch operators.

Jio is considering deploying a low-Earth-orbit satellite to deliver internet services from space, a venture that would put it in direct competition with Elon Musk’s Starlink , which has been seeking regulatory approval to enter India for years.

Reliance Group has also invested in the United States. Last month, Ambani took State Secretary Marco Rubio to tour the largest oil refinery at the Jamnagar facility, where both discussed processing more Venezuelan oil.

Musk, the world’s richest man and also a key ally of US President Donald Trump, recently hit out at Ambani.

His Starlink space telecommunications firm has struggled for years to secure a licence to operate in India.

In ⁠a series of X posts, Musk accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government of stalling Starlink’s entry to ⁠favour market leader Ambani’s telecom firm, Jio.

Musk taunted Ambani directly, addressing ‌him as “Prime ‌Minister Ambani” and asking whether he would “consider allowing Starlink to compete”. Starlink, Musk wrote, was being blocked by “oligarchs” protecting their “monopolistic chokehold” on Indians.

In a statement issued on X, Reliance said it has “never feared competition” and has “grown in an India that welcomes investment and innovation, homegrown or international”.

articles.title: California police investigate deadly shooting at Spirit Halloween store
articles.summary: Seven people suffered gunshot wounds at a Spirit Halloween store inside Fairfield's Solano Town Center on Halloween eve, with no arrests made.
articles.body: One person was killed and at least six others were injured in a shooting at a Spirit Halloween store in Fairfield, California, on Friday evening, the eve of Halloween. The Fairfield Police Department said officers responded to reports of a shooting around 8:30 p.m. local time at the Spirit Halloween store inside the Solano Town Center shopping mall. Police confirmed that seven people suffered gunshot wounds, including one who later died from their injuries. The six surviving victims were taken to local hospitals, with at least three in critical condition, according to police. MULTIPLE PEOPLE WOUNDED IN SHOOTING AT SOUTH CAROLINA'S LARGEST MALL; AUTHORITIES DETAIN SUSPECTS Authorities did not immediately release the identities of the victims. "Our thoughts and prayers are with the families of the victims of this heartbreaking incident," police said in a statement. Police did not immediately provide information about a suspect or suspects, but said detectives were working with witnesses to identify those responsible. TALLAHASSEE POLICE ARREST 15-YEAR-OLD SUSPECT AFTER SHOOTING NEAR FLORIDA A&M FOOTBALL STADIUM No arrests had been announced in connection with the shooting. Police are asking anyone with information about the shooting to contact the Fairfield Police Department at 707-428-7600 or email 1030mall@fairfield.ca.gov. articles.title: Private jets, yachts and powerful friends helped Alexander brothers lure women — and silence them, lawyer says
articles.summary: Private jets, superyachts and mansions helped the Alexander brothers lure sex trafficking victims into their orbit, an attorney told Fox News Digital.
articles.body: Jets, superyachts, mansions and access to the rich and powerful helped the Alexander brothers lure women into their orbit while creating an "aura" that left victims afraid they would not be believed, an attorney representing three women pursuing civil claims against the convicted sex traffickers told Fox News Digital. Alon, Oren and Tal Alexander were each sentenced in New York Tuesday to 30 years in federal prison for a yearslong sex-trafficking scheme that prosecutors said relied in part on the brothers' wealth, social status and luxury lifestyle to lure women before drugging and sexually assaulting them. But the sentences that capped their federal prosecution do not mark the end of the legal reckoning facing the brothers. ANDREW, TRISTAN TATE ARRESTED IN MIAMI AS UK SEEKS EXTRADITION ON EXPANDED RAPE, TRAFFICKING CHARGES Michael J. Willemin, a partner at Wigdor LLP, told Fox News Digital that his firm represents three women pursuing civil claims against the brothers and said evidence revealed during the federal prosecution could bolster allegations made in those cases. Willemin said the brothers surrounded themselves with wealthy and powerful people while using their lavish lifestyle to attract women and build an image that made victims fearful of coming forward. WOMEN ACCUSE PEARADISE FOUNDER OF PREYING ON THEM BY TURNING ‘SAFE SPACE’ INTO MANSION OF MANIPULATION "They used things like luxury trips and parties and introductions to celebrities and powerful individuals and private jets and super yachts, mansions and estates," Willemin said. Those trappings, he said, served as "a compliment in some ways to the drugs and the alcohol that were used to impair the memory of their victims and ultimately allowed them to get away with this sort of behavior for as long as they did." CORNELL SEXUAL ASSAULT CASE REVIVES SCRUTINY OF A LITTLE-KNOWN NEW YORK LAW ON INTOXICATED VICTIMS Prosecutors said the brothers used their wealth and prominence to create opportunities to sexually assault women between at least 2008 and 2021. Women were identified through social media, dating apps, in-person encounters and party promoters before being offered luxury experiences, travel and accommodations. On multiple occasions, prosecutors said, women were then drugged and forcibly raped or sexually assaulted, sometimes by multiple men. CONVICTED SERIAL RAPIST ORIGINALLY SENTENCED TO 124 YEARS WALKS FREE AFTER 20, SPARKING OUTRAGE Assistant U.S. Attorney Andrew Jones described it during closing arguments as a "consistent playbook to lure, isolate and rape their victims." Willemin said the brothers' wealth and access did more than help draw women into their social circles. He said it also heightened fears about what could happen if victims accused them publicly. "There's an added layer of concern that the women who come forward are going to be retaliated against," Willemin said. That could include fears of being pushed out of social circles, being surveilled or facing other potentially violent behavior, he said. HARVEY WEINSTEIN SENTENCED TO 15 YEARS IN PRISON FOR 2006 SEX CRIME IN NEW YORK "That's something that is a very real fear for women that is exacerbated when someone can use wealth and power to help secure silence," Willemin said. Willemin represents Angelica Parker, who sued all three brothers in 2024, along with Samantha Fields and a Jane Doe who have brought separate civil claims. MAX FACTOR HEIR'S FORMER LAWYER DETAILS JUDGE'S ERROR THAT WIPED OUT 124-YEAR RAPE SENTENCE Parker alleges Oren invited her and a friend to the New York City apartment he shared with Tal and Alon in 2012, where Oren and Alon offered the women ecstasy, which they declined. After Parker's friend left the apartment, Parker alleges Alon and Tal sexually assaulted her together while Oren watched. JUDGE GRILLS AG’S OFFICE IN CORNELL SEX ASSAULT CASE AS EX-FRAT BRO’S LAWYER DEMANDS OUSTER OVER ALLEGED BIAS The allegations in Parker's lawsuit are separate civil claims and were not adjudicated by the federal jury that convicted the brothers. Willemin said evidence that emerged during the criminal prosecution nevertheless supports Parker's contention that what allegedly happened to her was planned rather than spontaneous. "There was a whole host of evidence with respect to text messages and videos and other behaviors that suggested that these sexual assaults were not the random acts of spontaneity, but were, in fact, planned, which help also support the allegation made by Ms. Parker," Willemin said. The federal prosecution may now also change the landscape for the remaining civil cases. Willemin said Parker's case has progressed further than the other two his firm is handling and is moving through an appeals process involving whether older sexual assault claims can proceed. An argument is scheduled in January before the New York Court of Appeals over legal issues Willemin said could determine the outcome of numerous civil cases against the brothers. "The civil cases are moving forward now," Willemin said. "And one of the sort of roadblocks to that was to have the criminal case completed. That's now obviously completed to a degree and now the civil cases should be able to move forward." FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X When asked whether additional women may have been victimized but never publicly came forward, Willemin said, "I wouldn't doubt that at all." "It would be, you know, frankly, pretty surprising if every woman who had been the victim of a sexual assault by the Alexander brothers has come forward, given the evidence that we have as far as how widespread this occurred," Willemin said. At Tuesday's sentencing, the brothers continued to deny drugging, raping or trafficking women while acknowledging and expressing regret for past attitudes and comments about women. SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS Federal prosecutors had sought life sentences, while defense attorneys asked for the mandatory minimum of 15 years. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB U.S. District Judge Valerie Caproni ultimately sentenced each brother to 30 years in prison, followed by 10 years of supervised release. Alon and Oren were each fined $300,000, while Tal was fined $350,000. SEND US A TIP For Willemin's clients, the federal sentences represent only one part of what they are seeking. GOT A TIP? His firm hopes to move its three civil cases through discovery and ultimately to trial, where Willemin said his clients want juries to recognize that they were wronged and provide a remedy through the civil justice system. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST "The criminal convictions were welcome for sure, and the sentence, although it could have been longer, it could have been life, was also significantly longer than the minimum sentence that could have been given," Willemin said. articles.title: DEPROGRAMMED: Ex-Palestine supporter blasts 'insane' movement for 'cherry-picking' oppressors
articles.summary: Parishad Kavyani says Palestinian supporters cherry-pick between oppressors and stay silent on Iranian women wanting freedom and basic rights.
articles.body: Parishad Kavyani was born in the Islamic Republic of Iran and spent most of her childhood there until she moved to Canada at 14, a reality she says shaped her nuanced view of the pro-Palestine, anti-Israel movement she once supported. Now she says it was destroyed by "liberal intellectualism" that overly focused on the oppressor instead of the human rights of all affected. "I have never faced the amount of homophobia, racism and sexism that I have experienced in the past nine months from the leftists, from the very people that I marched with for over two years for a free Palestine, and that is insanity," Kavyani told Fox News Digital of leaving the cause. Kavyani went on to reveal one of the problems she wrestled with while still supporting the Palestine movement — the absence of support for the freedom and rights of Iranian women. IRANIAN-AMERICAN DOCTOR SENDS FIERY MESSAGE TO HOLLYWOOD ACTRESS AS IRAN PREPARES TO EXECUTE FEMALE PROTESTER "[They] advocate for liberation of people, [they] advocate for women's rights, but when it comes to Iranian women wanting freedom, wanting the freedom to wear whatever they want, [they] suddenly are quiet — and not only quiet, but [they] support the oppressor. That's my issue… [they] cherry-pick between oppressors," she said. Kavyani, who admits to being a part of pro-Palestine when the movement began to form before splitting with the cause after an array of its supporters began posting pro-Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps [IRGC] content, detailed the intricate view Iranians develop on advocacy for Palestinians. "As an Iranian born and raised in Iran… you are raised with a lot of information, a lot of propaganda around what is happening in Israel, what is happening in Palestine, and you are just told this every single day by the authorities. That Palestinians need help, they've been oppressed, they've been getting killed all of these years, so we have to help them," she added. INSIDE TEHRAN: IRANIANS DESCRIBE IRGC'S BRUTAL RULE, POVERTY — ASK TRUMP TO 'STAY THE COURSE' "Then… you enter the society, and you see there is poverty everywhere. You see that the villages in Iran don't have drinking water. You see that the villagers in Iran don’t have a road to a hospital… Why? Because the government doesn't actually do anything about the people in need inside the country, and you're always told, ‘Oh, but we have to save money to send to Palestine,’" Kavyani said. "The more time you spend in the country you’re like, ‘Why is it my responsibility to save another nation?’" Kavyani added. The Hamas terrorist attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, was a tipping point for her. "When October 7 happened, I had a lot of conversations with people [about it]... Like, just because someone is holding an Israeli passport doesn't mean that they should just get killed… If there’s a war that you're including civilians in that war, and you're taking civilians hostage, and you're raping civilians or torturing civilians — that's not something that I support no matter who this person is, because I'm not somebody who thinks someone deserves to die just because of where they're from or just because the political belief that they hold on to," she said. HASAN PIKER'S DEFENSE OF HAMAS HAVING 'RIGHT TO RESIST MILITARILY' DRAWS CONDEMNATION FROM HUMAN RIGHTS GROUPS "That is, like, so ideology-driven, which we're seeing right now on the internet and in real life… You cannot create a hierarchy of people and say this person deserves saving more than this person… That liberal intellectualism is, like, so insane," Kavyani relayed. After it happened, she said, she saw a fundamental flaw in the coalition to which she once considered herself connected, saying they were "cherry-picking" between killers. "After that happened, I started separating myself… because I was like, this is not the group that I want to associate myself with because I don't think a lot of the people within that movement are there for the human rights aspect of it," Kavyani said. articles.title: Florida Gators look to strengthen College Football Playoff case in ranked matchup with Georgia
articles.summary: Florida and Georgia clash with College Football Playoff and Conference Championship implications as the Gators try to avoid a costly third loss.
articles.body: There are only about five games remaining for most teams before we start to get into Bowl season and the Conference Championship games. There has been a ton of fluctuation on the Top 25 this season, with very few teams looking like a confident option to make it into the College Football Playoffs. Florida and Georgia play today, and a win here for Florida would go a long way for its case and probably hurt the Bulldogs quite a bit. The Florida Gators are 5-2 for the season, with both losses coming in SEC games. This has been a hard team to judge this year. The Gators have had some really good games, and then a few ugly ones. Their best game came when they destroyed the Ole Miss Rebels. That was a ranked matchup, at home, and they took down the team with a solid 52-28 victory. Unfortunately for them, their success was rather short-lived. The next week against Missouri, they lost 45-17, barely even showing up for the game. It didn’t get any better the following week as they lost that game 38-19 to South Carolina. That’s a game they will want back at the end of the year. articles.title: Canada cracks down on immigration fraud; agents face penalties of up to Canadian $1.5 million
articles.summary: New rules target unauthorised immigration advisers and representatives who submit false information, with Indian students and aspiring migrants among
articles.body: New rules target unauthorised immigration advisers and representatives who submit false information, with Indian students and aspiring migrants among those who could benefit from stronger safeguardsCanada has introduced stringent financial penalties for immigration and citizenship fraud, with individuals and organisations providing unauthorised immigration advice or knowingly submitting false information facing penalties of up to C$1.5 million.The new measures, which came into force on Oct 28, are aimed at protecting prospective immigrants and citizens from fraudulent immigration advisers, unlicensed agents and dishonest representatives who exploit applicants seeking study permits, work permits, permanent residence and citizenship.Under the new framework announced by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC), a person providing paid immigration or citizenship advice or representation without the required authorisation can face a penalty of Canadian $5,000. Those who knowingly provide false or misleading information on behalf of an applicant, or help an applicant do so, can face penalties of Canadian $15,000.Additional penalties may apply if an application is approved on the basis of false or misleading information. The penalties can increase for repeat violations, with the cumulative maximum reaching Canadian $1.5 million.Importantly, the measures apply not only to unlicensed immigration agents but also to authorised representatives, including licensed immigration consultants and lawyers, who engage in prohibited conduct. They apply irrespective of whether the representative operates within or outside Canada.Lena Metlege Diab, immigration minister said: “Anyone hoping to build a future in Canada deserves access to trustworthy and accurate immigration and citizenship advice. These new measures will help protect people from fraud and misconduct and hold those who break the law accountable. While most people providing paid advice and representation follow the rules, those who do not will face consequences. This will help protect applicants and strengthen the integrity of Canada’s immigration and citizenship systems.”Indian students caught in fake admission letter scandalThe crackdown comes against the backdrop of several immigration fraud investigations involving Indian nationals, particularly students aspiring to study in Canada.One of the most significant cases came to light in 2023, when some Indian students already in Canada faced enforcement action after Canadian authorities discovered that fraudulent letters of acceptance from educational institutions had been submitted with their study permit applications.The issue prompted a joint task force involving IRCC and the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA). According to figures presented by the Canadian government, more than 2,000 cases were initially examined. Indian nationals accounted for 89% of the cases, followed by Vietnamese nationals at 8% and Chinese nationals at 3%.However, the figures did not mean that all those investigated had knowingly committed fraud. Canadian authorities acknowledged that some students could have been victims of unauthorised immigration consultants who supplied fraudulent admission letters without their knowledge.According to media updates, of the 285 individuals brought within the scope of the task force, 108 cases had been reviewed by Feb 22, 2024. Sixty-seven individuals were identified as genuine students, 40 as non-genuine, while one case required further review.The issue resurfaced in India in June 2025 when Jalandhar police arrested Brijesh Mishra, accused of running a fake admission letter racket through an immigration consultancy. Police alleged that more than 200 students aspiring to study in Canada had been duped through forged college offer letters.Fraud has been reported in cases of individuals seeking employment and permanent residence in Canada.Public naming of penalised representativesAn important feature of the new framework is the proposed public disclosure of enforcement action. IRCC plans to publish the names of penalised representatives and details of their violations on its website. A public registry is expected to be launched in 2027, after the first penalties have been administered.The new financial penalties also complement separate regulatory changes that took effect on July 15, 2026, strengthening the oversight of immigration and citizenship consultants. These changes expanded the investigative and disciplinary powers of the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants and established a compensation fund for victims of dishonest consultants.Applicants remain responsible for their applicationsCanadian immigration authorities have repeatedly warned applicants that using an agent does not absolve them of responsibility for the information submitted in their name.Submitting fake or altered documents, including admission letters, employment offers, educational qualifications and language test results, can lead to refusal of an application and a ban on entering Canada for at least five years. In certain circumstances, an individual's existing immigration status or even citizenship can be revoked.IRCC advises applicants to check whether a paid representative is authorised, obtain a written contract and receipts, avoid signing blank application forms and ensure that they review the complete application before submission.For thousands of Indians aspiring to study, work or settle in Canada, the new rules serve as a reminder that an attractive immigration promise from an agent can come at a considerable cost if the underlying application is fraudulent.You use AI every day. articles.title: Florida conservationist spent five decades protecting forests and wildlife; his efforts helped save thousands of acres of wilderness; now a trail honours his legacy
articles.summary: For more than five decades, Florida conservationist Bob Simons worked to protect forests, preserve wildlife habitats and prevent ecologically sensitive
articles.body: For more than five decades, Florida conservationist Bob Simons worked to protect forests, preserve wildlife habitats and prevent ecologically sensitive landscapes from being lost to development. A forester and longtime member of the Alachua Audubon Society, Simons contributed to efforts to protect thousands of acres across north-central Florida, including land that became part of San Felasco Hammock Preserve State Park. He also devoted nearly three decades to building and maintaining nest boxes for the Southeastern American kestrel, one of the smallest falcons in the United States. Although Simons died in June 2024, his conservation work continues to be recognised. In October 2026, a new observation platform and a trail at Turkey Creek Preserve were dedicated in his honour, celebrating a lifetime spent protecting Florida's natural heritage.How he helped protect thousands of acres of wildernessDuring the early 1970s, Simons identified an ecologically sensitive mixed-hardwood forest in north-west Gainesville that he believed deserved protection. He persuaded 10 private landowners to sell their properties to the state and spent two years lobbying legislators to support the effort.His campaign contributed to the establishment of San Felasco Hammock Preserve State Park, which covers approximately 6,900 acres and protects a diverse range of natural habitats. The preserve is known for its hardwood forests, wildlife and extensive network of trails.Simons also contributed to conservation efforts involving other natural areas across Florida, including River Rise Preserve State Park, Silver Springs State Park, Tosohatchee Preserve and Fakahatchee Strand Preserve State Park. His work extended to Pinhook Swamp, an ecologically important landscape associated with the connection between Florida's Osceola National Forest and Georgia's Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge.His achievements formed part of broader conservation efforts involving public agencies, environmental organisations, landowners and local advocates. Together, these efforts helped protect natural landscapes that might otherwise have faced development or other forms of land-use change.Three decades devoted to protecting a tiny falconAlongside his work to preserve forests, Simons devoted nearly three decades to protecting the Southeastern American kestrel, one of the smallest falcons in the United States.He spent years constructing, installing, maintaining and repairing nest boxes to provide suitable nesting sites for the birds. He also acquired a telescoping camera to help monitor activity inside the boxes, supporting efforts to understand their nesting behaviour.The project involved college interns and volunteers, giving them opportunities to participate in wildlife monitoring and conservation work. Simons' long-term commitment reflected the importance of sustained observation and practical intervention in protecting wildlife.His work with the kestrel also demonstrated how conservation extends beyond protecting large landscapes. Providing suitable nesting sites, monitoring wildlife and maintaining habitats can all contribute to efforts to support vulnerable species.His work helped shape local conservation policySimons' influence extended beyond individual parks and wildlife projects. He was a longstanding advocate for policies that protected ecologically sensitive areas from intensive development.He opposed large-scale construction on environmentally important land and challenged proposals that would have permitted activities such as grazing, timber harvesting and hunting in state parks. He also supported prescribed burning, a land-management practice used in suitable ecosystems to maintain habitats and reduce accumulated vegetation.According to the Alachua Conservation Trust, Simons' surveys and documentation of natural communities helped provide a scientific foundation for the Alachua County Forever programme. The initiative focuses on protecting environmentally significant land, including areas important for water resources, wildlife habitats and natural landscapes.Turkey Creek Preserve: land protected from developmentOne of the places associated with Simons' conservation legacy is Turkey Creek Preserve, a roughly 375-acre natural area in Alachua County, Florida. The land had been designated for another phase of residential development, but conservation efforts helped preserve it as a natural landscape.Today, the preserve contains a variety of habitats, including basin swamp, depression marsh, dome swamp, upland hardwood forest, blackwater streams and sinkholes. These environments support wildlife and contribute to the area's ecological value.The preserve is also home to the state-endangered woodland poppy mallow and the state-threatened gopher tortoise. Its walking trails allow visitors to experience the area's forests and wetlands while observing its natural features.Alachua County acquired the preserve in December 2009, using funding from its Wild Spaces Public Places sales tax programme, alongside reimbursement through the Florida Communities Trust. Its protection reflects the combined efforts of public agencies and conservation advocates to safeguard environmentally important land.The preserve now offers visitors an opportunity to experience the kind of natural landscape Simons spent decades working to protect.A new trail and observation platform honour his legacyOn October 3, 2026, approximately 60 people, including county officials, conservationists, friends and family, gathered at Turkey Creek Preserve to honour Simons and celebrate the opening of a new wildlife observation platform.The ceremony also marked the dedication of the Blue Trail in his honour. The route leads visitors on a walk of roughly half a mile to the observation platform, providing an opportunity to explore the preserve's natural surroundings.Interpretive signs along the trail explain aspects of Simons' conservation work, including his involvement in the Champion Tree programme and his efforts to protect the Southeastern American kestrel. The platform gives visitors a place to observe the surrounding wetlands and wooded habitats.The dedication creates a lasting tribute to Simons at a preserve that reflects the wider conservation mission he championed. It also allows visitors to learn about the people and sustained efforts behind the protection of natural landscapes.Why the ceremony ended with a vine cuttingOne detail from the dedication ceremony offered a glimpse into Simons' approach to the natural world. Instead of a conventional ribbon-cutting, the event concluded with a vine-cutting ceremony.According to WUFT's report, Simons believed vines played an important ecological role and should not simply be pulled down from trees. The unusual ceremony reflected his appreciation for the complexities of natural ecosystems and the need to understand them before intervening.His wife, Erika Simons, attended the dedication, joining those who gathered to recognise his decades of conservation work. For friends and fellow conservationists, the event was an opportunity to remember both his achievements and his commitment to protecting Florida's natural heritage.A legacy that extends beyond one trailBob Simons' conservation legacy encompasses the natural areas he helped protect, the wildlife projects he sustained and the environmental programmes he supported over more than five decades.His involvement in efforts to establish and protect natural areas, including San Felasco Hammock Preserve State Park, helped shape conservation work across north-central Florida. His long-running kestrel nest-box project also demonstrated the value of sustained commitment to wildlife protection.The trail and observation platform at Turkey Creek Preserve now give visitors a way to learn about his work while experiencing the habitats conservationists strive to preserve. They serve as a reminder that protecting wilderness often requires years of research, advocacy and cooperation, and that the effects of such work can endure long after the people behind it are gone.You use AI every day. articles.title: Women may have a biological edge over men when tasting bourbon, experts say
articles.summary: Women have nearly 50% more olfactory neurons than men, giving them a scientific edge in detecting bourbon's vanilla, cinnamon and leather notes, according to experts.
articles.body: There's a theory in the bourbon world that women are better at tasting the spirit than men, and some experts say there's scientific proof to back up the claim. Smelling is an important step in the tasting process, and there is some evidence that suggests women have an advantage in that area. "Women have a keener sense of smell and taste than men," Louisville, Kentucky-based whiskey expert and author Susan Reigler told Fox News Digital. WINE EXPERT SAYS ONE COMMON HABIT COULD BE SABOTAGING EVERY SIP Reigler, who is also a former president of the Bourbon Women organization, cited a scientific paper published in 2014 that explored the differences in the olfactory bulbs of men and women. The report showed that women have just under 50% more neurons than men in olfactory regions, a difference that could contribute to a stronger sense of smell. "There are a number of different factors that come to play and certainly things that are outside of smell that affect men and women differently," Caitlin McLean, the vice president of Qualitative Solutions at MMR Research Worldwide's North American offices in New York, told Fox News Digital. NEW 123.4-PROOF WHISKEY PROMPTS EXPERT WARNING THAT STRONGER ISN'T ALWAYS BETTER McLean noted that there's more to tasting bourbon than just what happens in the mouth and on the palate. The processes of orthonasal and retronasal olfaction play big roles in the tasting experience. Orthonasal olfaction occurs when aromas enter through the nostrils, such as smelling aromas, while retronasal olfaction occurs when those aromas "are coming up in sort of the back of your palate and hitting the nose from the inside," McLean explained. "When we think about what's critical to bourbon, some of those distinctive notes, like vanilla and cinnamon and leather and tobacco, smoke, dark fruit, all of those are identified through retronasal olfaction," she said. Hormones also come into play, too, McLean noted, especially estrogen, which is associated with a heightened sense of smell. "So in moments of pregnancy or menopause, you do see strong differentiation in olfactory sensitivity," McLean said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS The belief that women are better bourbon tasters is partially rooted in the idea that women are biologically wired to have a stronger sense of smell and taste as a way to protect their children, a theory that is difficult to prove with data. "There is some scientific evidence that women, on average, outperform men in olfactory tasks, but maternal instinct is a difficult one to prove scientifically," McLean said. articles.body: Jamshedpur: A 20-year-old woman has alleged that she was raped inside a police station in Seraikela-Kharsawan district on the intervening night of Thursday and Friday. articles.title: Iran warns of unfettered retaliation if attacked as mediators try for peace
articles.summary: Iran’s supreme leader says Tehran’s potential response will not be restricted by geography.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has issued a strongly worded message to the Iranian armed forces, as mediators continue to try to prevent a new breakout of war between Iran and the United States.

Senior diplomats from Qatar held extensive talks in Tehran on Friday , with further talks expected to take place on Saturday.

Iranian authorities say they are prepared to respond forcefully amid reports that the US and Israel are preparing for new strikes on Iran.

The office of Iran’s Supreme Leader, Khamenei, who has not been seen or heard from since replacing his assassinated father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, in March, said on Saturday that he met with senior military commanders and gave them “important strategic directives”.

Khamenei required “maximum deterrence” through preparedness for “an immediate and effective response, without geographical restriction” if the country is attacked again, according to a statement released by the office.

It comes days after US Vice President JD Vance wrote a letter to Tehran, reportedly addressed to Mohsen Rezaei, the Supreme National Security Council leader who has become a central power in strategic decision-making in Iran despite failing over decades to garner enough votes for public office.

Exact details of the letter are unclear, but Vance is believed to have called for nuclear commitments from Iran, including allowing international inspectors to monitor the country’s nuclear programme and determining the fate of Iran’s highly enriched uranium, which Tehran has said will not be shipped abroad .

US President Donald Trump earlier rejected reports that he had ordered renewed peace talks, instead claiming without elaborating that the Vance letter was concerned with allowing medical supplies into Iran.

According to Iranian media, Tehran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within several days in exchange for a return to the June memorandum of understanding still remains the baseline for the mediated negotiations.

Tehran’s demands include the lifting of a US maritime blockade on Iranian ports, waivers on oil sanctions, and a truce for regional conflicts, including in Lebanon where Israeli forces continue to occupy the country’s south.

Local media confirmed that Iran received the letter, although they did not say whether any official response has been given through mediators.

An Iranian state-linked Jomhouri-e Eslami (“Islamic Republic”) newspaper published an editorial on Saturday saying that even though the chances of reaching an agreement with the US were slim and fighting could break out after the US midterm elections on November 3, it was still imperative to give a positive response to negotiations and meetings over the coming days.

“We must not allow war to be accepted as the inescapable fate for Iran,” it said.

Iran and the US have kept up their attempts to assert control in the Strait of Hormuz. The IRGC has continued attacking ships and warns of a lingering threat from alleged naval mines. The US military provides guidance and cover for a shuttle system to get oil from Arab states out of the waterway.

Local authorities reported on Saturday afternoon that two fishing boats were bombed by a US drone south of Qeshm island in southern Iran, wounding several fishermen.

Iranian state television claimed late on Friday that at least six tankers, including a very large crude carrier bearing two million barrels of oil, were damaged by explosions after allegedly hitting mines in recent days while transiting “unauthorised” routes in the strait. It also released footage recorded from a small boat close to a larger vessel that was dealing with a fire.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) on Friday reported a new type of attack that occurred a day earlier. It said a tanker was approached by a small boat which attached two explosive devices to the hull above the waterline, resulting in a blast that caused a fire in the engine room and temporarily disabled the vessel northeast of Oman’s Khasab.

The maritime monitor said it recorded 155 inbound and 122 outbound transits through the Strait of Hormuz in the week ending October 28, which was 70 percent lower than pre-war levels.

In a video message on Friday, US Central Command chief Brad Cooper said he flew over the strait and saw dozens of vessels carrying cargo, crude oil and liquid natural gas while being supported by US aircraft and sea drones.

“I didn’t see the IRGC out there at all,” he said. “They patrolled the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters for decades, harassing and threatening and seizing commercial vessels at will. But they were not out there because Iran’s navy is all at the bottom of the sea.”

The rhetoric coming from Tehran has only hardened after eight months of war. In line with Khamenei’s Saturday statement, army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia warned the Trump administration against attacking Iran.

“If the US president once more embarks on adventurism in the region through threats and greed of the Zionists, the fire of war will undoubtedly engulf a wider geography,” he said, in reference to Israel.

Other senior officials took aim at Washington’s European allies, who expressed backing for both the US-Israeli offensive on February 28 and last year’s 12-day war.

After German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the costs of war had exceeded 100 billion euros for Europe over the past eight months. Iran’s security chief Rezaei said Europe was “whining” now even though it cheered the war earlier.

“When you cheered on war crimes, did you think the fallout wouldn’t hit you, too? War and terror come at a price. Now it’s your turn to pay,” he wrote on X.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also reminded that Merz had celebrated Israel and the US “doing the dirty work” for Europe during last year’s war.

“100bn Euro is nothing compared to the Earth-shattering blow Iran’s Powerful Armed Forces will deal against those who dare harm our people,” he wrote. “Red lines are a thing of the past”.

US Senator Chris Murphy said earlier this week that he had a meeting with senior officials about what a short and blistering US military campaign would look like if the war resumes.

“Their plan is insane. It will lead to devastating escalation and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law,” he said.

Eric Brewer, deputy vice president for the Nuclear Materials Security Program for the US-based Nuclear Threat Initiative, said it is entirely unclear what would be achieved through extensive air strikes against Iran’s infrastructure, considering that Trump earlier this week bemoaned that Iran has focused on rebuilding after earlier attacks.

“There is no military solution for remaining nuclear sites [Pickaxe, Esfahan tunnels], and the program remains generally paused. Striking energy targets is unlikely to cause Iran to capitulate to US negotiating demands,” he wrote on X, adding that Iran will also retaliate across the region if attacked.

“They will aim to make the war not just more painful for the US and its partners, but longer than we would prefer,” Brewer said. “The risks of this operation far exceed any gains.”
